Apply the Work at Height Regulations 2005 — ensure access is planned, the access equipment is appropriate and in good condition, and a colleague or contact is aware of the inspection. Never use an unfooted ladder alone. For roof-mounted plant, carry out a specific risk assessment before accessing the roof — fragile roofing materials, leading edge falls, and unstable surfaces are common hazards.

Plant rooms and confined spaces

Plant rooms are a common feature of capital allowances surveys — boiler rooms, electrical switch rooms, generator rooms, and basement plant areas. Some plant rooms constitute confined spaces under the Confined Spaces Regulations 1997 — spaces that are substantially enclosed, where there is a reasonably foreseeable risk of serious injury from hazardous substances or conditions. Assess whether any plant room constitutes a confined space before entering and apply the appropriate controls — do not enter a confined space alone, ensure adequate ventilation, and have rescue arrangements in place.

Asbestos in commercial buildings

Asbestos is present in a significant proportion of commercial and industrial buildings constructed before 2000. Before carrying out any intrusive inspection check whether an asbestos register exists for the property and review it. Do not disturb any suspected asbestos-containing materials. Common locations for asbestos in commercial buildings include pipe lagging, ceiling tiles, floor tiles, roofing sheets, and plant room insulation — all areas that may be relevant to a capital allowances survey. If asbestos is identified that may affect the survey seek specialist advice before proceeding.

Lone working

Capital allowances surveys are frequently carried out alone. Before any solo site inspection ensure a colleague knows your location and expected return time. Carry a fully charged mobile phone. Confirm the site contact details in case of emergency. For large or complex sites — extensive industrial premises, multi-storey buildings with numerous plant rooms — consider whether a site contact should accompany you throughout the inspection.

Manual handling and survey equipment

Capital allowances surveys may require carrying survey equipment — laser measures, cameras, tablets, and reference materials — around large and complex sites. Apply manual handling risk assessment principles — do not carry excessive loads, use appropriate bags and equipment carriers, and take regular breaks on extended surveys. On industrial sites be aware of uneven surfaces, trailing cables, and other manual handling hazards that may not be obvious in an office environment.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of health and safety knowledge in your capital allowances survey work. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you identified and managed a health and safety risk during a survey — not generic descriptions of following a risk assessment. Prepare examples from your own experience covering at least two of the hazard categories above — assessors will ask for specific situations, not general principles.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Capital Allowances Practice
sections.body:
Module 6 covered accounting principles at a general level. On the Taxation Allowances pathway, accounting principles are a core competency to Level 3 — the highest mandatory level. This reflects the fundamental role that tax accounting plays in capital allowances practice. Your competency examples for this area must demonstrate reasoned advice, not just practical application.

How capital allowances interact with tax accounts

Capital allowances are a form of tax relief — they reduce the taxable profit of a business by allowing a deduction for capital expenditure on qualifying assets. The capital allowances claim is prepared by the surveyor, reviewed by the tax adviser, and submitted to HMRC as part of the tax return. The surveyor identifies and values the qualifying expenditure — the tax adviser incorporates that into the tax computation and manages the HMRC relationship. Understanding how capital allowances interact with the tax computation is essential for advising clients competently and for working effectively alongside tax advisers.

The capital allowances pool structure

Capital allowances are claimed through pools. The main pool attracts a writing down allowance of 18% per year on the reducing balance. The special rate pool attracts a writing down allowance of 6% per year — a significantly slower rate of relief. Integral features (electrical systems, cold water systems, space or water heating systems, lifts, escalators, and external solar shading) go into the special rate pool at 6% WDA. Long-life assets with an expected useful life exceeding 25 years also go into the special rate pool. The practical consequence of the special rate pool is that the tax relief on integral features is delivered much more slowly than on main pool plant — this affects the net present value of the capital allowances benefit and is an important consideration in claim strategy advice.

Annual Investment Allowance

The Annual Investment Allowance provides 100% first-year relief on qualifying plant and machinery expenditure up to the AIA limit — currently £1 million per year. AIA can be claimed on both main pool and special rate pool expenditure but not on cars or assets acquired for leasing. Where capital expenditure exceeds the AIA limit in a single year the order of allocation — which expenditure goes against AIA and which goes into the pools — affects the timing of the tax relief. Advising clients on AIA utilisation and the optimal allocation of expenditure against the AIA is a core business planning skill.

Structures and Buildings Allowance

The Structures and Buildings Allowance was introduced in October 2018 and provides a 3% straight-line allowance on qualifying expenditure on new commercial structures and buildings — or the improvement of existing ones. SBA does not apply to residential property, land, or plant and machinery — it covers the structural element of commercial construction and refurbishment that would not otherwise attract capital allowances. Understanding the boundary between plant and machinery allowances and SBA is a key technical skill — correctly classifying expenditure between the two regimes directly affects the rate of tax relief available.

The interaction between accounts depreciation and capital allowances

Capital allowances replace accounts depreciation for tax purposes. A business adds back its accounts depreciation charge in the tax computation and claims capital allowances instead. This means the capital allowances position can differ significantly from the accounts position — particularly in the early years of an asset's life where AIA provides 100% first-year relief that accounts depreciation would spread over the asset's useful life. Understanding this interaction is essential for explaining the tax benefit of a capital allowances claim to a client and for advising on the timing of capital expenditure decisions.

Reading a capital allowances tax computation

Capital allowances practitioners must be able to read and interpret a capital allowances tax computation. The computation shows the pool balances brought forward, the additions in the year (new qualifying expenditure), the disposals in the year (proceeds from the sale of qualifying assets), the AIA claimed, the WDA claimed at the appropriate rate, and the pool balance carried forward. Anomalies in the computation — unusually low WDA claims, missing disposal entries, incorrect pool allocations, or a main pool balance that does not reconcile with the capital expenditure history — are the starting point for identifying missed capital allowances opportunities on historic instructions.

Balancing allowances and balancing charges

When a qualifying asset is disposed of, the disposal proceeds are deducted from the pool balance. If the disposal proceeds exceed the pool balance a balancing charge arises — effectively a clawback of excess allowances previously claimed. If the pool balance exceeds the disposal proceeds a balancing allowance may arise in certain circumstances — principally on the cessation of a business or on the disposal of a short-life asset. Understanding balancing allowances and balancing charges is essential for advising clients on the tax consequences of asset disposals and business cessations.

APC Level 3 application — reasoned advice

Remember that on this pathway Accounting principles and procedures is required to Level 3 — not Level 2. Your competency examples must demonstrate that you provide reasoned advice on accounting matters — advising a client on the optimal AIA allocation strategy, explaining the tax computation impact of a capital allowances claim, or identifying anomalies in a historic computation that indicate missed allowances. Assessors will probe your understanding of the tax accounting framework in depth. Prepare examples that show you understand the link between the capital allowances claim and the client's overall tax position.

sections.h: 11B.5 Capital Allowances Data Sources and Professional Tools
sections.body:
Capital allowances practice relies on a specific set of data sources and professional tools that are not used in general surveying practice. Competent use of these tools is expected at APC Level 2 — assessors will ask you which sources you used in specific instructions and why.

The HMRC Capital Allowances Manual

The HMRC Capital Allowances Manual is the primary reference for capital allowances practitioners. It sets out HMRC's interpretation of the Capital Allowances Act 2001 and provides guidance on the treatment of specific items of plant and machinery, the fixtures legislation, the pooling requirement, and disputed areas. Key sections include CA11000 (plant and machinery — general), CA21000 (meaning of plant), CA22000 (meaning of machinery), CA26000 (integral features), CA28000 (long-life assets), and CA29000 (short-life assets). Candidates must be familiar with the structure of the manual and be able to navigate it to find guidance on specific items — assessors will expect you to know which sections of the manual are relevant to contested items.

The Capital Allowances Act 2001

The CAA 2001 is the primary legislation governing capital allowances. Key sections include section 11 (entitlement to allowances), section 21 (buildings — exclusion), section 22 (structures — exclusion), section 23 (the list of items that are not excluded despite being in or on a building), section 33A (integral features), and sections 172 to 204 (fixtures). Candidates must be familiar with the structure of the Act and understand the key provisions that govern qualification and apportionment. The ability to cite the relevant section of the Act when explaining your treatment of a specific item is a mark of genuine technical depth.

Case law

Capital allowances case law is an essential data source for practitioners. HMRC's manual cites case law extensively and contested items are frequently resolved by reference to decided cases. Key cases candidates must know include: Yarmouth v France (1887) — established the functional test for plant, that an asset is plant if it is used for carrying on a business and is not merely the setting in which the business is carried on; Wimpy International v Warland (1988) — applied the setting test to restaurant fit-out, distinguishing between items that are plant and items that are merely the setting; and J Lyons and Co v Attorney General (1944) — the premises test, distinguishing between the structure of a building and the plant within it. Candidates should be familiar with the leading cases and understand the principles they establish.

Construction cost data

Quantifying and apportioning construction expenditure between qualifying and non-qualifying elements requires access to construction cost data. Primary sources include: the contractor's own cost breakdown or final account — the most reliable source where available; the quantity surveyor's cost plan or final account on new construction projects; BCIS (Building Cost Information Service) — the primary published source of construction cost data for RICS members; and published price books including Spons and Laxton's. Where the contractor's cost breakdown does not provide sufficient detail for capital allowances apportionment, elemental cost analysis using BCIS data is the standard methodology.

Valuation data and apportionment evidence

Where capital allowances claims involve the apportionment of a property purchase price between land, structures, and plant and machinery, valuation data is required. Sources of valuation evidence include comparable sales data, yield-based valuations of the income-producing element, and residual valuations. The s198 election mechanism — a written agreement between vendor and purchaser on the apportionment of the purchase price — removes the need for a formal valuation in many cases, but where the election value is disputed or where no election has been executed, a formal valuation apportionment is required. Candidates must understand both the valuation methodology and the legislative framework that governs apportionment.

The HMRC portal and agent access

Capital allowances claims are submitted to HMRC as part of the corporation tax return or self-assessment return through the HMRC online portal. Capital allowances practitioners with agent status can access client tax records, review historic computations, and liaise with HMRC directly through the portal. Understanding the agent access system and the process for submitting and amending capital allowances claims is an important practical skill. Candidates should understand the submission process even if the actual filing is handled by the tax adviser.

Specialist capital allowances software

Several specialist software platforms have been developed for capital allowances practitioners — these assist with the identification, quantification, and apportionment of qualifying expenditure, the preparation of the capital allowances schedule, and the documentation of the claim. Candidates should be familiar with the tools used in their firm's practice and be able to explain how they support the claim preparation process and maintain the audit trail required for HMRC enquiry defence.

Survey and measurement tools

Capital allowances surveys require accurate measurement and documentation of plant and machinery. Laser distance measurers, digital cameras, and tablet-based survey applications are standard tools. Photographic evidence of plant and machinery is essential for HMRC enquiry defence — photographs should be clearly labelled with the location, the item, and the date of inspection. Measurement data supports the quantification of mechanical and electrical services where a detailed contractor breakdown is not available.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate that you use appropriate data sources in your professional work. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you consulted the HMRC Capital Allowances Manual, applied case law principles to a contested item, used construction cost data to apportion expenditure, or used valuation data to support a purchase price apportionment. Assessors will ask which sources you used in specific instructions — be precise and explain why each source was relevant to that instruction.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Capital Allowances Instructions
sections.body:
Module 3 covered client care principles at a general level. Capital allowances instructions involve a specific multi-adviser dynamic that creates client care challenges not encountered in most other surveying contexts. Managing these relationships professionally is a core skill for Taxation Allowances pathway candidates.

The multi-adviser relationship

Capital allowances instructions almost always involve multiple professional advisers — the surveyor, the tax adviser (accountant or tax solicitor), and sometimes a specialist capital allowances consultant. The surveyor's role is the technical identification and quantification of qualifying expenditure — the tax adviser's role is the tax computation and HMRC submission. Misunderstandings about the boundary between these roles are a common source of dispute and client dissatisfaction. Confirm your scope of work in writing at the outset of every instruction and ensure the client and tax adviser understand clearly what you will and will not be doing. Never allow scope creep to draw you into giving tax advice that falls outside your competence and professional indemnity cover.

Corporate clients and procurement processes

Many capital allowances instructions are for corporate clients — property investors, developers, owner-occupiers, and occupational tenants. Corporate clients typically have formal procurement processes, finance approval requirements, and multiple internal stakeholders. Understanding the corporate client's decision-making structure — who has authority to instruct, who approves expenditure, who will sign off on the claim — is essential for managing the instruction effectively. Identify the key stakeholders at the outset, confirm their roles, and maintain regular communication with all relevant parties throughout the claim preparation process.

Managing client expectations on claim value

A common client care challenge in capital allowances practice is managing expectations about claim value. Clients — and sometimes their tax advisers — may have unrealistic expectations about the quantum of qualifying expenditure, influenced by marketing claims from aggressive capital allowances promoters. Your professional obligation is to prepare an accurate and defensible claim — not to maximise the claim at the expense of accuracy. When a client's expectations exceed what is defensibly supportable, explain clearly why, document your advice in writing, and be prepared to lose the instruction rather than prepare a claim that will not stand up to HMRC scrutiny. An inflated claim that triggers an HMRC enquiry causes significantly more damage to the client relationship than a conservative but accurate claim.

Supporting clients through HMRC enquiries

When a capital allowances claim is subject to HMRC enquiry, the client will look to you for support and reassurance. Managing the client relationship during an enquiry requires clear communication — explaining the enquiry process, setting realistic expectations about timeline and outcome, and keeping the client informed of progress. Liaise closely with the tax adviser throughout the enquiry and ensure that all responses to HMRC are consistent and coordinated. Your file must be maintained to a standard that allows you to reconstruct and defend every element of the claim — poor file management is one of the most common reasons practitioners cannot support their clients effectively during enquiries.

Conflict of interest in capital allowances practice

Capital allowances instructions create specific conflict of interest risks. The most common is the s198 election situation — where you are instructed by both vendor and purchaser in a property transaction that requires an agreed apportionment of the purchase price between qualifying and non-qualifying elements. Vendor and purchaser have directly opposing interests in the election value — the vendor wants a low value to minimise any balancing charge, the purchaser wants a high value to maximise the qualifying expenditure available for claim. Acting for both parties in this situation is a conflict of interest that must be identified and managed before accepting the instruction. In most cases the appropriate course is to act for one party only and recommend that the other instructs independent advisers.

Contingency fee arrangements

Capital allowances practitioners frequently work on a contingency fee basis — a percentage of the tax saving generated by the claim. Contingency fee arrangements must be clearly documented in the terms of engagement with the basis of calculation, the percentage rate, the trigger for payment, and the method of calculation all confirmed in writing. Be aware of RICS guidance on contingency fees — fees must be fair and reasonable and must not create perverse incentives to inflate claims. Where a contingency arrangement means your fee increases if the claim quantum increases, document carefully how you have maintained objectivity and accuracy in your claim preparation.

Written terms of engagement

All capital allowances instructions must be confirmed in writing with a clear scope of work, fee basis, liability cap, and confirmation of who you are acting for. Review your terms of engagement for every instruction — do not rely on a standard letter that has not been updated to reflect the specific scope of the work. For contingency fee instructions, the terms of engagement are particularly important — they define the relationship between the claim outcome and your fee and must be watertight to avoid disputes on completion.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of client care principles in capital allowances instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you managed a multi-adviser relationship, set and managed client expectations on claim value, supported a client through an HMRC enquiry, or identified and managed a conflict of interest. Prepare examples that show genuine professional judgement in managing complex client relationships — not just a description of following standard procedures.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning for Capital Allowances Practices
sections.body:
Module 7 covered business planning at a general level. For Taxation Allowances pathway candidates, business planning applies both to the strategic advice you give clients on the use of capital allowances within their property and business strategies, and to the development of your own capital allowances practice.

Capital allowances as a strategic business planning tool

Capital allowances are not just a tax compliance exercise — they are a significant strategic tool for property investors, developers, and owner-occupiers. The timing and structuring of capital expenditure can significantly affect the tax position of a business over multiple years. Advising clients on the capital allowances implications of their property strategy — acquisition timing, refurbishment planning, lease restructuring, and disposal — requires an understanding of both the technical rules and the client's broader business objectives. When advising on a property acquisition the capital allowances analysis should be part of the pre-acquisition due diligence, not an afterthought added once the transaction has completed.

Pre-acquisition capital allowances reviews

A pre-acquisition capital allowances review assesses the capital allowances position of a property before exchange — identifying the historic qualifying expenditure, the pool history, the fixtures that may qualify under the fixtures legislation, and the s198 election strategy. This review informs the purchaser's bid strategy — the value of the capital allowances available affects the after-tax cost of the acquisition — and ensures the s198 election is negotiated correctly at the point of sale. A pre-acquisition review that identifies significant unclaimed or transferable capital allowances can be one of the most commercially valuable pieces of advisory work a Taxation Allowances practitioner delivers. Candidates must be able to structure, conduct, and present a pre-acquisition review with confidence.

The s198 election strategy

Where a property changes hands the fixtures legislation requires the vendor and purchaser to agree how the purchase price is apportioned between qualifying plant and machinery fixtures and the non-qualifying elements. This agreement is recorded in a s198 election. The election value determines the qualifying expenditure the purchaser can claim — and the balancing charge or allowance position of the vendor. Poorly negotiated s198 elections — or failing to execute an election altogether — can result in significant lost capital allowances for the purchaser and unexpected tax consequences for the vendor. Advising clients on s198 election strategy, supporting the negotiation, and ensuring the election is correctly executed and submitted to HMRC is a core business planning skill.

Refurbishment and fit-out planning

Capital allowances planning for refurbishment and fit-out projects can significantly enhance the tax efficiency of the investment. Identifying qualifying plant and machinery at the design and specification stage — rather than after completion — allows the project team to maximise the qualifying proportion of the expenditure. Working with the design team and quantity surveyor during the project to ensure qualifying items are separately identified in the cost plan and final account is far more efficient than retrospective apportionment from a lump-sum final account. Advising clients to engage a capital allowances specialist at the design stage — and making that case persuasively to clients and their project teams — is a key piece of strategic business planning advice that distinguishes proactive practitioners from reactive ones.

AIA utilisation and expenditure timing

The Annual Investment Allowance provides 100% first-year relief on qualifying expenditure up to £1 million per year. Advising clients on how to maximise AIA utilisation — including the timing of capital expenditure relative to the accounting year end, the allocation of expenditure between AIA and the pools, and the interaction between AIA and the special rate pool — is a practical business planning skill with direct cashflow implications for the client. Where a client's capital expenditure in a year exceeds the AIA limit, the order of allocation determines how quickly the remaining expenditure attracts relief — allocating special rate expenditure against AIA first maximises the rate of relief on main pool expenditure that would otherwise attract 18% WDA.

Historic claims and look-back reviews

Many properties have never had a capital allowances survey carried out — or had one carried out many years ago when the technical standards were lower. A look-back review of historic qualifying expenditure can identify significant unclaimed allowances that can be brought into the tax computation in the current year. Advising clients on the availability and commercial value of a look-back review — and managing the risk that HMRC may scrutinise a large one-year claim representing many years of historic expenditure — is a business planning skill that requires both technical knowledge and commercial judgement.

Practice development and referral relationships

Capital allowances is a specialist and competitive market. Building and maintaining referral relationships with accountants, tax advisers, solicitors, and commercial agents is essential for practice development. Understanding what each referral source needs from you — prompt turnaround, clear fee structures, technical credibility, reliable claim quality — and managing those relationships professionally is a business skill that goes beyond technical expertise. Candidates who can demonstrate awareness of the commercial dynamics of their practice, and who have contributed to its development, will stand out in their APC assessment.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of business planning principles in capital allowances instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you provided strategic capital allowances advice — a pre-acquisition review, s198 election strategy advice, refurbishment planning input, AIA utilisation advice, or a look-back review — not just routine claim preparation. Assessors will look for evidence that you understand the strategic value of capital allowances within a client's broader property and business strategy.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Capital Allowances Practice
sections.body:
Module 8 covered conflict avoidance and dispute resolution at a general level. Capital allowances practice has specific dispute contexts — primarily involving HMRC — that candidates must understand and manage proactively.

HMRC enquiries — the primary dispute context

The most significant dispute context in capital allowances practice is an HMRC enquiry into a submitted claim. HMRC may open an enquiry into the capital allowances schedule of a tax return — questioning the qualification of specific items, the apportionment methodology, or the quantum of the claim. An enquiry is not an accusation of wrongdoing — it is a formal investigation process — but it requires a thorough, well-documented, and professionally managed response. The best way to avoid an enquiry becoming a protracted dispute is to prepare claims to HMRC enquiry standard from the outset — clear methodology, case law support for contested items, documented inspection evidence, and a defensible apportionment approach. When an enquiry is opened engage with HMRC promptly and professionally, provide the information requested clearly and completely, and seek specialist tax dispute resolution support if the enquiry cannot be resolved through normal correspondence.

Preparing claims to enquiry standard

Every capital allowances claim should be prepared as if it will be subject to HMRC enquiry. This means: documenting the inspection methodology and the basis for including or excluding each item; maintaining photographic evidence of all plant and machinery inspected; recording the case law authority for the treatment of contested items; documenting the apportionment methodology and the data sources used; and maintaining a complete correspondence file. A claim file that cannot withstand an HMRC enquiry is a claim that should not have been submitted. The discipline of preparing to enquiry standard from the outset is the single most effective conflict avoidance tool in capital allowances practice.

s198 election disputes

Disputes over s198 election values are a common source of conflict between vendors and purchasers. The vendor typically wants a low election value — minimising any balancing charge on disposal — while the purchaser wants a high election value — maximising the qualifying expenditure available for claim. Where the parties cannot agree the default position under the fixtures legislation applies — an outcome that is generally unfavourable to both parties. Early negotiation of the election value, supported by professional advice on both sides, is the most effective way to resolve election disputes. Where agreement cannot be reached through negotiation, RICS expert determination provides a binding resolution mechanism that is faster and less expensive than litigation.

The pooling requirement

The fixtures legislation includes a pooling requirement — a purchaser can only claim capital allowances on fixtures if the vendor has previously brought the fixtures into their own capital allowances pool. Where a vendor has never claimed capital allowances on fixtures — perhaps because no survey was carried out at the time of their acquisition — the purchaser may be unable to claim allowances on those fixtures regardless of the election value agreed. Identifying the pooling history of a property before exchange — through the pre-acquisition review process — is the most effective way to avoid discovering a pooling problem after the transaction has completed.

Disputes with tax advisers

Capital allowances practitioners sometimes face disputes with tax advisers about the technical treatment of specific items or the quantum of the claim. These disputes arise most commonly where the tax adviser has their own view on what qualifies — perhaps based on a different reading of the HMRC manual or a different interpretation of case law — or where the tax adviser is under pressure from the client to increase the claim quantum. Manage these disputes professionally — present your technical analysis clearly, cite the relevant legislation and case law, and document your position in writing. Where you cannot agree on the treatment of a specific item, recommend that both positions are set out clearly in the claim documentation so that HMRC can make the determination if necessary.

Professional negligence risk

Capital allowances practitioners face a specific professional negligence risk — claims arising from missed capital allowances opportunities or from claims that are successfully challenged by HMRC. A purchaser who did not obtain a pre-acquisition capital allowances review, or who executed a s198 election at an undervalue without professional advice, may seek to recover their loss from the adviser who handled the transaction. Maintaining clear written terms of engagement that define the scope of your advice — and ensuring that any limitations on your scope are clearly communicated to the client — is the most effective risk management tool. Professional indemnity insurance must be maintained at an appropriate level for the value of claims being handled.

RICS dispute resolution services

RICS DRS provides mediation, adjudication, arbitration, and expert determination services relevant to capital allowances disputes. Expert determination is particularly appropriate for disputes about the quantum of a capital allowances claim or the value of a s198 election — the appointment of an independent expert with specialist capital allowances knowledge provides a quick, binding, and cost-effective resolution. Mediation is appropriate for multi-party disputes involving clients, tax advisers, and HMRC where the relationship between the parties needs to be preserved.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of conflict avoidance principles in your capital allowances practice. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you managed an HMRC enquiry, negotiated a s198 election dispute, identified a pooling problem before it became a dispute, or managed a professional negligence risk through clear documentation and terms of engagement. Prepare examples that show professional judgement in managing conflict — not just a description of the dispute resolution options available.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability and Energy-Efficient Plant
sections.body:
Module 10 covered sustainability at a general level. Capital allowances practice has a specific and important relationship with sustainability — the tax system uses capital allowances as a mechanism to incentivise investment in energy-efficient and low-carbon plant and machinery. Taxation Allowances pathway candidates must understand both the technical capital allowances treatment of sustainable plant and the policy context that drives client demand for this advice.

The policy context — net zero and commercial property

The UK government's legally binding net zero target by 2050 is driving significant investment in energy-efficient and low-carbon plant and machinery in commercial property. Building owners are decarbonising their property portfolios — replacing fossil fuel heating systems with heat pumps, installing solar generation and battery storage, upgrading building management systems, and investing in EV charging infrastructure. Each of these investments generates capital allowances claims — and the Taxation Allowances practitioner is well-placed to advise clients on the tax efficiency of their decarbonisation investment. Understanding the policy drivers behind client capital expenditure decisions is essential for positioning your advice effectively.

Electric vehicles and charging infrastructure

Electric vehicles qualify for 100% first-year allowances — a significant tax incentive for businesses transitioning their vehicle fleets away from fossil fuels. EV charging infrastructure installed at commercial premises also qualifies for capital allowances — the specific treatment depends on whether the charging points are integral features or standalone equipment. Charging points that are part of the building's electrical infrastructure — hard-wired into the building's distribution system — are likely to be integral features qualifying for the special rate pool at 6% WDA. Standalone charging units that can be relocated are more likely to qualify as main pool plant at 18% WDA. Correctly classifying EV charging infrastructure is an increasingly common instruction as businesses invest in fleet electrification.

Solar panels and renewable energy plant

Solar panels installed on commercial buildings qualify as plant and machinery for capital allowances purposes — they are not structures and therefore not subject to the building exclusion in s21 CAA 2001. The capital allowances treatment of solar panels and other renewable energy plant on commercial properties is a well-established area of practice. Battery storage systems associated with renewable energy installations also qualify as plant and machinery. The interaction between capital allowances and the business rates treatment of renewable energy plant is an area where clients may need coordinated advice from rating and capital allowances advisers — be aware of the potential interaction and flag it where relevant.

Heat pumps and low-carbon heating systems

Heat pumps and other low-carbon heating systems are increasingly common as building owners decarbonise their property portfolios. The capital allowances treatment requires careful analysis of the system components. Air source and ground source heat pump units are generally plant and machinery qualifying for main pool allowances. The pipework and heat distribution systems associated with them — underfloor heating pipework, radiator circuits, fan coil units — may be integral features qualifying for the special rate pool as space or water heating systems. The ground loops of a ground source heat pump system present an interesting classification question — they are below ground and connected to the building's heating system, but their primary function is heat exchange rather than structural support. Correctly classifying each component of a low-carbon heating system requires the same technical analysis as any other building services installation.

Building management systems and smart controls

Building management systems — the computerised control systems that manage a building's heating, cooling, ventilation, lighting, and security — qualify as plant and machinery for capital allowances purposes. As buildings become smarter and more energy-efficient, the BMS becomes an increasingly significant element of the fit-out cost and therefore an increasingly important element of the capital allowances claim. Smart meters, energy monitoring systems, and demand-side response technology also qualify as plant and machinery where they are installed in commercial premises. Candidates should be confident in identifying and classifying BMS and smart control systems in capital allowances surveys.

Green leases and sustainability obligations

Green leases — leases that include obligations on landlord and tenant to manage the property in an environmentally sustainable way — are becoming increasingly common in commercial property. Capital allowances practitioners advising on refurbishment projects covered by green lease obligations must understand how the sustainability requirements affect the scope and specification of the works — and therefore the quantum and classification of the qualifying expenditure. Works carried out to comply with green lease energy efficiency obligations are generally qualifying plant and machinery expenditure where they involve the installation or replacement of building services plant. Understanding the green lease context helps practitioners identify the full scope of qualifying expenditure on sustainability-driven refurbishment projects.

The Future Buildings Standard and energy efficiency investment

The government's Future Buildings Standard and the trajectory toward net zero commercial buildings is driving significant investment in energy-efficient plant and building services. This investment generates capital allowances claims — and Taxation Allowances practitioners are well-placed to advise property owners on the tax efficiency of their decarbonisation investment. Understanding the policy context — the net zero target, the Future Buildings Standard, the minimum energy efficiency standards for commercial lettings — helps practitioners position their advice within the client's broader sustainability strategy and identify capital expenditure that may not otherwise have been identified as a capital allowances opportunity.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of sustainability principles in your capital allowances practice. Your competency examples should include specific instances where sustainability considerations affected your capital allowances advice — advising on EV charging infrastructure, solar panels, heat pumps, BMS upgrades, or other low-carbon plant and machinery. Assessors will ask about specific sustainability-related instructions from your experience. The intersection of capital allowances and the net zero agenda is a live and growing area of practice — candidates who can demonstrate awareness of this context and apply it to real instructions will stand out.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
You have now covered the nine substantive areas of Taxation Allowances pathway preparation. Before you move to Module 12 and your final assessment preparation, this section gives you the opportunity to practise Taxation Allowances-specific APC scenarios with Michael — both in Tutor Mode to consolidate your understanding and in Assessor Mode to experience the kind of questioning you will face in your final assessment.

How to use Michael for Taxation Allowances APC preparation

Michael has full knowledge of the Taxation Allowances pathway — competency selection rules, the six core competency requirements, the Capital Allowances Act 2001 structure and key sections (s11, s21, s22, s23, s33A, and the fixtures provisions at ss172–204), the HMRC Capital Allowances Manual and its key chapters, the three leading cases (Yarmouth v France 1887, Wimpy International v Warland 1988, and J Lyons and Co v Attorney General 1944), the pool structure (main pool at 18% WDA, special rate pool at 6% WDA, AIA at 100% up to £1 million, SBA at 3% straight-line), the fixtures legislation and s198 elections, the pooling requirement, integral features under s33A, the interaction between capital allowances and tax accounts, and current HMRC practice on contested items.

In Tutor Mode, Michael will explain concepts, work through scenarios with you, help you structure your competency examples, and identify gaps in your knowledge. Use Tutor Mode when you want to develop your understanding — ask him to explain the functional test, walk you through the application of the s23 list to a specific office refurbishment, or help you articulate your Level 3 Capital allowances competency evidence.

In Assessor Mode, Michael will challenge you exactly as a panel assessor would — direct questions, follow-up questioning, testing the depth behind your initial answer, probing your professional judgement on technical and ethical matters. Use Assessor Mode when you want to test your readiness — ask him to run a mock interview on your core competency, challenge your plant classification reasoning, or probe your understanding of the fixtures legislation.

Suggested Taxation Allowances APC practice scenarios

Work through as many of these as you can before moving to Module 12. Each scenario tests a different aspect of your Taxation Allowances pathway preparation:

  • Competency selection — Describe your six core competencies and your two optional choices to Michael. Ask him to challenge whether your optional selections reflect your actual day-to-day work and whether they are evidenced at the right level. Ask him specifically about the Accounting principles and procedures competency — why it is required to Level 3 on this pathway and what that means for the depth of your competency examples.
  • Plant and machinery classification — Ask Michael to work through the capital allowances treatment of a recently refurbished office: raised access floors, suspended ceilings, demountable partitions, and the air conditioning system. Ask him to identify the relevant section of the CAA 2001, the applicable case law, and the correct pool allocation for each item. Ask him to follow up on the distinction between plant and machinery and integral features, and the practical consequence of the pool allocation for the rate of tax relief.
  • The s23 list — Ask Michael to test your knowledge of section 23 CAA 2001 — the list of items that are not excluded despite being in or on a building. Ask him to follow up on specific items: general lighting, partitioning, raised floors, cold water systems, and fire suppression systems. Ask him to probe the boundary between s23 items and integral features under s33A and the practical implications for pool allocation.
  • s198 election strategy — Ask Michael to present a scenario where you are acting for a purchaser of a commercial investment property. The vendor has previously claimed capital allowances and the pooling requirement is satisfied. Ask Michael to test your knowledge of the election mechanism, the vendor's and purchaser's interests, the default position if no election is executed, and the tactical considerations in negotiating the election value. Ask him to follow up on the consequences of an undervalued election for the purchaser's long-term capital allowances position.
  • HMRC enquiry response — Ask Michael to present a scenario where HMRC has opened an enquiry into a capital allowances claim you submitted two years ago, questioning the qualification of partitions, raised floors, and items claimed under the s23 list. Ask him to test your knowledge of the evidence required to defend the claim, how you would structure your response to HMRC, and how you would manage the client and tax adviser relationship during the enquiry. Ask him to follow up on the consequences of failing to maintain adequate inspection records at the time of the survey.
  • Sustainability — Ask Michael to test your knowledge of the capital allowances treatment of a ground source heat pump installation and an EV charging infrastructure project. For the heat pump, ask him to distinguish between the main pool and special rate pool treatment of different system components. For the EV charging, ask him to test the distinction between integral features (hard-wired charging points) and standalone equipment. Ask him to follow up on the interaction between capital allowances and business rates for solar panels on a commercial building.
  • Pre-acquisition review — Ask Michael to present a scenario where a client is acquiring a commercial investment property and asks you to carry out a pre-acquisition capital allowances review. Ask him to test your knowledge of what the review should cover — the pool history, the fixtures position, the pooling requirement, and the s198 election strategy. Ask him to follow up on how you would advise the client if you discover the pooling requirement has not been satisfied for a significant element of the qualifying expenditure, and how you would present your findings and recommendations clearly.

Common Taxation Allowances referral patterns

Based on APC assessment experience, these are the areas where Taxation Allowances candidates are most commonly referred:

  • Shallow knowledge of the CAA 2001 — candidates who cannot cite the relevant sections when explaining the treatment of specific items, or who are unable to navigate the Act to find the provision that applies. Assessors on this pathway expect practitioners to know the key sections of the CAA 2001 and to be able to apply them accurately under questioning.
  • Inability to apply the functional and setting tests — candidates who can state the tests from Yarmouth v France and Wimpy International v Warland but cannot apply them to specific items under questioning. The tests are applied item by item to the specific facts — candidates who offer only generic descriptions without demonstrating their application will not satisfy an assessor on this pathway.
  • Poor understanding of the fixtures legislation — candidates who are unaware of the pooling requirement, who cannot explain the consequences of failing to execute a s198 election, or who do not understand the vendor's and purchaser's positions in an election negotiation. The fixtures legislation is a core element of Taxation Allowances practice and is tested in depth at every assessment.
  • Outdated or incomplete technical knowledge — candidates who are unaware of the Structures and Buildings Allowance, who quote an incorrect AIA limit, or who cannot describe current HMRC practice on commonly contested items. This pathway requires current knowledge — assessors will probe the detail.
  • Generic client care answers — candidates who describe the general principles of client care without demonstrating knowledge of the specific challenges of capital allowances instructions — the multi-adviser dynamic, the HMRC enquiry support role, the conflict of interest risks in s198 election situations, and the management of client expectations on claim quantum. Generic answers to client care questions are a reliable indicator of a candidate who has not developed their practice in depth.

Review your performance against these common referral patterns. If any of them apply to you return to the relevant sections of Module 11B and use Michael to address the gap before moving to Module 12.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
This assessment tests your readiness to move from mandatory competency preparation into your final APC simulation in Module 12. It covers all nine substantive areas of Module 11B — competency selection, health and safety, accounting, data sources, client care, business planning, conflict avoidance, sustainability, and APC practice.

Work through the questions honestly. Where you find gaps return to the relevant section and use Michael in Tutor Mode to consolidate your understanding before attempting Module 12.

Assessment questions

  1. Your competency selection includes Capital allowances to Level 3 and Accounting principles and procedures to Level 3 as core competencies. A colleague who has just completed their APC on the Commercial Real Estate pathway tells you that Accounting principles and procedures only needs to be evidenced to Level 2. How do you respond and why does this matter for your preparation?
  2. You arrive at a multi-storey office building to carry out a capital allowances survey. The facilities manager tells you that the roof plant area contains operational air handling units and that the basement plant room has been flagged as a potential confined space. Describe your approach to managing the health and safety risks before and during your inspection of both areas.
  3. A client asks you to explain the difference between the main pool and the special rate pool, and why it matters which pool an item goes into. What do you tell them, and what are the three categories of expenditure that must go into the special rate pool?
  4. During a capital allowances survey of a recently refurbished office you need to determine the treatment of the following items: raised access floors, suspended ceilings, demountable partitions, and the air conditioning system. For each item identify the relevant section of the CAA 2001, the applicable case law, and your conclusion on qualification and pool allocation.
  5. You are acting for a purchaser of a commercial investment property. The vendor has never claimed capital allowances on the property. Your pre-acquisition review suggests there is significant qualifying expenditure in the fixtures. What is the pooling requirement, how does it affect your client's ability to claim, and how do you advise them to proceed?
  6. HMRC has opened an enquiry into a capital allowances claim you prepared eighteen months ago. They are questioning the qualification of partitions, raised floors, and decorative features. Describe the evidence you would need to support your claim, how you would structure your response to HMRC, and how you would manage the client and tax adviser relationship during the enquiry.
  7. A property developer client is about to commence a major commercial refurbishment. They have not previously used a capital allowances specialist. Make the case for involving you at the design stage rather than after completion, and explain specifically what you would do during the project to maximise the capital allowances outcome.
  8. A client is installing a ground source heat pump system as part of a decarbonisation project. The system includes the heat pump unit, the ground loops, the distribution pipework, and the radiators. For each component explain the capital allowances treatment, the relevant pool, and the writing down allowance rate that will apply.
  9. Your client's tax adviser is pressing you to increase the quantum of a capital allowances claim by including items you consider to be non-qualifying decorative features. The tax adviser argues that HMRC rarely enquires into claims of this size and that the risk is acceptable. How do you respond and what do you do next?
  10. An assessor asks: "Tell me about the most technically challenging capital allowances instruction you have worked on — what made it challenging, what technical issues did you encounter, and how did you resolve them?" What makes a high-scoring answer to this question, and what are the most common referral mistakes candidates make when answering it?

After completing the assessment

Review your answers against the content in sections 11B.2 to 11B.9. For any question where you struggled return to the relevant section and use Michael in Assessor Mode to practise until you can answer confidently and with depth.

When you are satisfied with your performance across all ten questions you are ready for Module 12 — Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

sections.h: 11B.12 If You've Been Referred: What This Module Means for You
sections.body:
If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Taxation Allowances professional. It's specific, actionable feedback about what didn't land clearly enough in a particular interview, on a particular day, in front of a particular panel. Most successful resit candidates aren't relearning their pathway from scratch — they're closing specific gaps identified in their referral report.

How to use this module differently on a resit

  • Go back to your actual referral report before you start, and map its specific feedback points against the sections in this module — if your referral cited a gap in, for example, conflict avoidance or business planning, prioritise that section rather than working through everything in the original order
  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Taxation Allowances-specific material here

Referral rates on Taxation Allowances and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m11b.title: Building Surveying Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Pathway-specific preparation for Building Surveying candidates — professional practice, technical tools, and specialist knowledge for the APC final assessment.

sections.h: 11B.0 Understanding Your Technical Pathway Module
sections.body:
Before you work through the rest of Module 11B, it's worth understanding what this module actually is and why it sits where it does in your journey to Chartered status.

Modules 1 through 11 built your grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies — the ethics, client care, communication, health and safety, and business skills every RICS candidate needs, regardless of pathway. That knowledge is necessary, but it isn't sufficient on its own. Assessors don't just want to know that you understand client care in the abstract — they want to see you apply it specifically to the kind of work Building Surveying candidates actually do.

That's what this module is for. Everything from here through the end of Module 11B has been built and verified specifically against the current official RICS Building Surveying pathway guide — not a generic template with your pathway's name inserted. The competency structure, the legal and technical detail, and the Module 12 scenario at the end are all grounded in what Building Surveying candidates are genuinely tested on.

How to use this module well

  • Treat the competency structure section (11B.2) as your reference point when finalising your own declaration with your counsellor — it's a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it
  • Read every section with your own PDR experience in mind — the goal is connecting this material to what you've actually done, not memorising it in the abstract
  • Use Michael, your AI tutor, to pressure-test your answers on the scenarios that feel less familiar, not just the ones you're already confident on
  • Treat the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine practice interview question, not a reading exercise — actually formulate your answer before checking the model response

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain, in your own words, why Building Surveying candidates are tested the way they are — not just recite what the test covers.

sections.h: 11B.1 Introduction and Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
The Building Surveying pathway is one of the broadest and most technically demanding in the RICS portfolio. Building surveyors work across the full lifecycle of the built environment — from condition surveys and defect diagnosis to contract administration, project management, and dispute resolution. No other pathway requires the same breadth of technical knowledge across construction technology, building pathology, legal and regulatory compliance, and professional practice.

The APC assessment for Building Surveying reflects that breadth. Assessors will probe your technical knowledge of building defects, your ability to read and administer contracts, your understanding of planning and building regulations, and your professional judgement across a wide range of instructions. Generic preparation is not enough — Building Surveying candidates need pathway-specific depth across every mandatory competency area.

This module bridges that gap. By the time you complete M11B you will be ready for the technical question bank, the mock interview, and the APC assessment itself with confidence in both your technical knowledge and your ability to apply it under pressure.

Michael has full Building Surveying pathway knowledge built in — the December 2025 RICS requirements, building pathology and defect diagnosis, JCT contract forms, CDM regulations, planning and building regulations, Party Wall etc. Act 1996, fire safety, and current industry standards. Use him throughout this module and throughout your preparation.

Learning Outcomes

  • Explain the Building Surveying pathway competency structure and make informed competency selection decisions
  • Identify and manage health and safety risks specific to building surveying practice including CDM obligations
  • Apply accounting principles to building surveying instructions including construction cost management and final accounts
  • Use specialist building surveying data sources and professional tools accurately and confidently
  • Demonstrate client care skills appropriate to building surveying instructions across a range of client types
  • Prepare and administer building contracts and manage construction projects professionally
  • Identify and manage conflict in building surveying contexts including Party Wall disputes and contract administration disputes
  • Evidence sustainability competence through energy efficiency, retrofit, and low-carbon construction advice
  • Practise Building Surveying APC scenarios with Michael in both Tutor Mode and Assessor Mode

sections.h: 11B.2 The Building Surveying Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
The Building Surveying pathway has a substantial core competency list — six technical core competencies all required to Level 3, plus Fire safety required to Level 1. This reflects the breadth of technical knowledge expected of a chartered building surveyor.

Mandatory competencies

Common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway: Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

The core competencies

  • Building pathology — Level 3 (the defining diagnostic competency of the pathway)
  • Construction technology and environmental services — Level 3
  • Contract administration — Level 3
  • Design and specification — Level 3
  • Inspection — Level 3
  • Legal and regulatory compliance — Level 3
  • Fire safety — Level 1

Optional competency selection

Building Surveying candidates select two optional competencies to Level 2 from a grouped selection. The grouped optional rule requires candidates to choose ONE from the following group: Client care (to Level 3), Conflict avoidance, Health and safety (to Level 3), Inclusive environments, or Sustainability. Note that Client care and Health and safety can be taken to Level 3 within this group — unusual for optional competencies. Plus one further optional to Level 2 from the full technical list.

Fire safety at Level 1 — what it means

Fire safety is a core competency on this pathway but only to Level 1 — demonstrating knowledge and understanding. However fire safety can also be selected as an optional competency to a higher level where it forms a significant part of your day-to-day practice. If fire safety is central to your work — fire risk assessments, fire stopping, means of escape — consider whether taking it to Level 2 or 3 as an optional competency better reflects your experience.

Building pathology to Level 3 — the assessor's lens

Building pathology is the competency that defines Building Surveying more than any other. At Level 3 you must be able to provide reasoned advice on complex defects — diagnosing the cause, advising on remediation, and anticipating future problems. Assessors will probe your diagnostic methodology, your knowledge of specific defect types, and your ability to give a professional opinion under follow-up questioning. Your competency examples for building pathology must demonstrate genuine diagnostic depth — not just a description of defects observed.

What assessors expect

Building Surveying assessors are experienced practitioners who will test your technical knowledge rigorously. They will present defect scenarios and ask you to diagnose the cause. They will ask you to administer a contract under pressure — responding to a contractor's claim, assessing an extension of time, certifying payment. They will probe your knowledge of building regulations and planning legislation. And they will test your professional judgement in situations where the technical answer is clear but the client's interest is complex.

Ask Michael

Use Michael in Tutor Mode to talk through your competency selection before finalising your APC submission. Describe your day-to-day work and ask him to help you build a coherent and well-evidenced selection.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Building surveying involves working in and around construction sites, occupied buildings, and structures in various states of repair. Health and safety obligations are particularly significant on this pathway — not only as a mandatory competency but as a professional obligation under CDM and other legislation.

CDM Regulations 2015

The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 are the primary health and safety framework for construction projects. Building surveyors frequently act as Principal Designer, Designer, or Client adviser under CDM — each role carries specific legal duties. As Principal Designer you must plan, manage, monitor and coordinate health and safety during the pre-construction phase, and prepare and maintain the Health and Safety File. As Designer you must eliminate foreseeable risks during design and provide information about residual risks to the Principal Designer. You must understand which projects require a Principal Designer and Principal Contractor, what triggers the F10 notification to the HSE, and what the Health and Safety File must contain.

Building inspections and surveys

Carrying out building surveys and inspections involves specific hazards — working at height on roofs and in roof spaces, entering confined spaces such as basements and crawl spaces, exposure to hazardous materials including asbestos and lead paint, and inspection of structurally unsound elements. Before any survey assess the specific risks — review any available asbestos survey or register, check for structural instability, and plan your access to height carefully. Apply the Work at Height Regulations 2005 whenever ladder or roof access is required. Never enter a confined space without appropriate controls.

Asbestos

Asbestos is present in a very high proportion of buildings constructed before 2000 and remains the single biggest occupational health risk in the construction industry. Building surveyors must understand the duty to manage asbestos under the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 — the duty holder (usually the building owner or occupier) must identify asbestos-containing materials, assess their condition, and manage the risk. When carrying out surveys of pre-2000 buildings always check for an asbestos register, treat unknown materials as potentially containing asbestos, and do not disturb any suspected ACM without appropriate precautions. Refurbishment and demolition surveys must be carried out before any intrusive works on pre-2000 buildings.

Construction site safety

Building surveyors carry out contract administration on live construction sites. On every site visit confirm that you have been inducted, that you are wearing appropriate PPE (hard hat, high-visibility vest, steel-capped boots as a minimum), and that you understand the site rules. Never enter a construction site without induction. Be aware of specific hazards on site — excavations and trenches, working at height, moving plant and vehicles, overhead power lines, and temporary works. Your role as contract administrator does not exempt you from site safety obligations — you are responsible for your own safety and must set an example to others.

Party Wall surveys

Party wall surveys involve inspecting adjoining owner's properties to record their condition before and after construction works. This requires access to properties that may be occupied, in poor condition, or otherwise hazardous. Always carry out a pre-survey risk assessment, obtain the occupier's cooperation, and be alert to hazards including unstable structures, trip hazards, and aggressive occupants.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of health and safety knowledge in building surveying practice. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you applied CDM duties, managed asbestos risk, carried out a risk assessment before a survey, or managed site safety as a contract administrator. Assessors will probe the depth of your CDM knowledge in particular — know your duties under each role and be prepared to give specific examples.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 6 covered accounting principles at a general level. Building surveying practice has specific accounting contexts — construction cost management, interim valuations and certificates, final accounts, and the financial management of building contracts — that candidates must understand and apply.

Construction cost management

Building surveyors are frequently involved in managing the cost of construction projects — preparing cost plans, monitoring expenditure against budget, and advising clients on cost implications of design decisions. A cost plan is prepared at various stages of a project — from initial feasibility through to tender stage — and provides the client with a progressively more accurate forecast of the total project cost. Understanding the structure of a cost plan, the basis of the elemental cost rates used, and the contingency and risk allowances appropriate at each stage is essential for building surveying candidates involved in project work.

Interim valuations and payment certificates

Under JCT contracts the contract administrator assesses interim valuations submitted by the contractor and issues payment certificates to the employer. The interim valuation assesses the value of work properly executed to date, materials on site, and any other amounts due under the contract. The contract administrator must assess the valuation independently and fairly — not simply accepting the contractor's submission. Understanding the basis of valuation under different JCT forms, the payment notice and pay less notice regime under the Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 (as amended), and the consequences of failing to issue certificates on time is essential for candidates involved in contract administration.

Final accounts

The final account settles the total amount due to the contractor under the contract, taking into account all variations, loss and expense claims, fluctuations, and any other adjustments. Preparing or agreeing a final account requires a thorough understanding of the contract valuation rules, the assessment of variations, and the principles governing loss and expense claims. Candidates must be able to distinguish between variations that are instructed under the contract and changes that arise from the contractor's own decisions, and understand the financial consequences of each.

Variations and change management

Variations to building contracts — changes to the scope of work instructed by the contract administrator — have direct financial implications for both employer and contractor. Understanding how to value variations under different JCT forms (using bill rates, fair rates, or daywork), how to assess the preliminary costs associated with variations, and how to manage the cumulative financial impact of multiple variations is a core contract administration skill. Candidates must also understand the distinction between a variation and a claim — not every change the contractor identifies as additional cost is a variation under the contract.

Loss and expense

Under JCT contracts a contractor may be entitled to direct loss and expense where regular progress of the works has been materially affected by relevant matters — typically employer actions or inactions such as late information, delayed access, or variations. Assessing loss and expense claims requires an understanding of the heads of claim — preliminaries, plant, labour, subcontractor claims, overheads, and financing charges — and the evidence the contractor must provide to support each head. Many loss and expense claims are poorly substantiated — the contract administrator must assess each head on the evidence provided and not simply accept or reject the claim in total.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of accounting principles in building surveying instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you prepared a cost plan, assessed an interim valuation, managed variations, or contributed to a final account. Assessors will probe your understanding of the payment regime under the HGCRA, the assessment of variations, and the principles of loss and expense. Prepare examples that show you understand the financial management of a building contract, not just the technical construction aspects.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Building surveying practice relies on a range of specialist data sources and professional tools. Competent use of these tools is expected at APC Level 2 — assessors will ask which sources you used in specific instructions and why.

BCIS — Building Cost Information Service

BCIS is the primary source of construction cost data for building surveyors. It provides elemental cost analyses, tender price indices, location factors, and cost planning data. Candidates must be able to use BCIS data to prepare cost plans, benchmark tender prices, and advise clients on construction cost. Key data sets include the BCIS Elemental Standard Form of Cost Analysis, the BCIS All-in Tender Price Index, and the BCIS Rebuilding Cost data used for insurance reinstatement valuations. Understanding the limitations of BCIS data — the importance of adjusting for location, specification, and market conditions — is as important as knowing how to access it.

NBS (National Building Specification)

NBS is the primary tool for preparing building specifications in the UK. Building surveyors use NBS to prepare performance and prescriptive specifications for building works — specifying materials, workmanship standards, and testing requirements. NBS Chorus is the current cloud-based platform. Candidates involved in design and specification work must be familiar with NBS and understand how specifications interact with drawings and bills of quantities to define the contractor's obligations.

Planning portal and local authority resources

Building surveyors regularly advise on planning applications, permitted development rights, and building regulations applications. The Planning Portal provides access to permitted development rules, application forms, and local authority planning registers. The local authority building control department is the primary point of contact for building regulations applications — candidates must understand the full plans and building notice routes, the inspection regime, and the completion certificate process. Many building surveyors also work with Approved Inspectors (now Registered Building Inspectors under the Building Safety Act 2022) as an alternative to local authority building control.

The Building Safety Act 2022 and gateway process

The Building Safety Act 2022 introduced fundamental changes to the regulation of higher-risk buildings — those 18 metres or more in height or with seven or more storeys containing at least two residential units. The new gateway process requires design and planning approval from the Building Safety Regulator before construction begins, and occupation approval before the building is occupied. Building surveyors working on higher-risk buildings must understand the gateway process, the dutyholder roles under the Act, and the new competency requirements for those working on higher-risk buildings.

JCT contract suite

The Joint Contracts Tribunal publishes the standard forms of building contract most widely used in the UK. Building surveyors must be familiar with the main JCT forms — JCT Standard Building Contract (SBC), JCT Intermediate Building Contract (IBC), JCT Minor Works Building Contract (MW), JCT Design and Build Contract (DB), and JCT Measured Term Contract (MTC). Each form is appropriate for different project types and procurement routes — candidates must be able to advise clients on the appropriate contract form for their project and understand the key provisions of each form.

Party Wall etc. Act 1996

The Party Wall etc. Act 1996 governs works to party walls, party structures, and excavations near neighbouring buildings. Building surveyors frequently act as party wall surveyors — for building owners and adjoining owners — and must understand the notice requirements, the schedule of condition process, the award procedure, and the resolution of disputes between surveyors. The RICS guidance note on party wall legislation is an important reference document for practitioners.

Asbestos surveys and registers

Before any survey or inspection of a pre-2000 building candidates should check for an asbestos management survey or refurbishment and demolition survey. The duty to manage asbestos under the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 requires duty holders to maintain an up-to-date asbestos register. Candidates must understand the difference between a management survey (suitable for routine maintenance) and a refurbishment and demolition survey (required before intrusive works) and know when each type of survey is required.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate that you use appropriate data sources in your professional work. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you used BCIS data, prepared a specification using NBS, navigated the planning portal or building regulations process, or applied your knowledge of the JCT contract suite. Assessors will ask which tools and sources you used in specific instructions — be precise and explain why each was relevant.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 3 covered client care at a general level. Building surveying instructions involve a diverse range of client types — from individual homeowners to large corporate occupiers — and the client care skills required vary significantly across these different contexts.

Private residential clients

Many building surveyors carry out homebuyer surveys, building surveys, and schedule of condition inspections for private residential clients.
