These clients are often making the most significant financial decision of their lives and may have limited understanding of construction or surveying. Managing expectations carefully — explaining what the survey will and will not cover, what the report will tell them, and what its limitations are — is essential. Written terms of engagement for residential survey instructions must comply with RICS guidance and clearly set out the scope and limitations of the service. Be alert to the emotional dimension of residential property transactions — a significant defect identified in a survey can be devastating for a client who has committed emotionally to the purchase.

Commercial and corporate clients

Commercial clients — investors, developers, occupiers — have different expectations from residential clients. They are typically more commercially focused, more familiar with the surveying process, and more interested in the financial implications of your advice than the technical detail. Adapt your communication style accordingly — lead with the commercial implications of your findings and provide the technical detail in support. Corporate clients often have formal governance processes — be clear about who has authority to instruct, who approves expenditure, and who needs to be copied on correspondence.

Employer and contractor relationships in contract administration

The contract administrator in a JCT contract occupies a specific and legally defined role — they act as the employer's agent in some respects but must also act fairly and independently in others, particularly when certifying, assessing extensions of time, and valuing loss and expense. This dual role creates client care complexity — the employer client may expect the contract administrator to act solely in their interest, but the contract administrator has obligations to the contractor that must be maintained independently. Explaining this role clearly to employer clients at the outset — and maintaining the professional independence the role requires — is essential for effective contract administration and for managing the client relationship when the contractor makes claims.

Managing difficult clients

Building surveyors sometimes work with clients whose expectations exceed what is professionally deliverable — clients who want a survey report to support a price reduction they have already decided on, employers who want extensions of time refused regardless of the merits, or clients who want advice that exceeds your professional competence or indemnity cover. Managing these situations requires clarity about your professional obligations, willingness to have difficult conversations, and the ability to document your advice clearly when a client chooses to proceed contrary to your recommendation.

Complaints handling

All RICS regulated firms must have a complaints handling procedure. Building surveying generates a disproportionate number of professional negligence claims relative to other RICS pathways — most commonly arising from survey reports that failed to identify defects that subsequently became significant. Understanding your firm's complaints procedure, responding to complaints promptly and professionally, and maintaining complete file records that allow you to reconstruct your advice are essential risk management skills.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of client care principles across the range of building surveying instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you managed client expectations, adapted your communication style to a specific client type, maintained professional independence in a contract administration role, or handled a client complaint or difficult situation. Assessors will probe the depth of your client care experience — prepare examples that show genuine professional judgement, not just a description of following standard procedures.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 7 covered business planning at a general level. For Building Surveying candidates, business planning applies both to the strategic advice you give clients on building and construction projects and to the management of your own surveying practice.

Feasibility studies and project appraisals

Building surveyors are frequently asked to advise clients on the feasibility of building projects — refurbishment versus redevelopment, extension versus relocation, repair versus replacement. A feasibility study assesses the technical, financial, and programme implications of the available options and provides the client with a basis for decision-making. Key components include: a technical assessment of the existing building and its suitability for the proposed use; a cost estimate for each option based on BCIS data and local market conditions; a programme comparison; a planning risk assessment; and a recommendation with supporting rationale. The ability to structure and present a feasibility study clearly is a core business planning skill for building surveyors.

Procurement strategy

Advising clients on procurement strategy — how to organise the design and construction process to achieve their objectives — is a significant business planning skill. The main procurement routes available to building surveying clients include: traditional procurement (design then build, with a contract administrator); design and build (contractor takes responsibility for design and construction); management contracting; and construction management. Each route has different implications for cost certainty, programme, risk allocation, and client involvement. Candidates must be able to explain the key features of each procurement route and advise clients on the most appropriate approach for their specific project.

Programme and project management

Building surveyors managing construction projects must understand the principles of programme management — preparing and maintaining a construction programme, identifying the critical path, managing float, and assessing the impact of delays and variations on the programme. Tools such as Gantt charts and network analysis (precedence diagrams) are standard in building surveying practice. Candidates involved in project management must be able to assess contractor extensions of time claims against the programme and advise clients on the programme implications of their decisions.

Insurance and risk management

Building projects carry significant financial risks — cost overruns, programme delays, defects, and third party liability. Advising clients on appropriate insurance cover — contractor's all risks, public liability, professional indemnity, latent defects insurance — is a business planning skill that building surveyors are expected to demonstrate. Understanding the basics of each insurance type, when it is required, and how it is procured helps clients manage the financial risks of construction projects effectively.

Planned and preventive maintenance

Building surveyors advising property owners and occupiers on the long-term management of their buildings are expected to prepare planned maintenance programmes — setting out the maintenance activities required, their frequency, and their estimated cost over a planning period of typically five to ten years. A planned maintenance programme helps clients budget for maintenance expenditure, prioritise works, and avoid reactive maintenance that is typically more expensive than planned intervention. The RICS guidance on planned maintenance is a relevant reference document for candidates involved in this area of practice.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of business planning principles in building surveying instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you prepared a feasibility study, advised on procurement strategy, managed a construction programme, or prepared a planned maintenance programme. Assessors will look for evidence that you understand the strategic and financial dimensions of building projects, not just the technical construction aspects.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 8 covered conflict avoidance at a general level. Building surveying practice generates a specific and recurring set of disputes — particularly in contract administration and party wall practice — that candidates must understand and manage proactively.

Contract administration disputes

The most common source of conflict in building surveying practice is the administration of building contracts. Disputes arise most frequently over: extensions of time — whether the contractor is entitled to additional time and how much; loss and expense — whether the contractor has suffered direct loss and expense and the basis of assessment; variations — whether an instruction constitutes a variation under the contract and how it should be valued; and payment — whether interim certificates fairly reflect the value of work carried out. The most effective way to avoid contract disputes is rigorous contract administration from day one — clear instructions in writing, prompt certification, fair and consistent decision-making, and complete records of all communications and decisions. When disputes do arise the JCT contract provides adjudication as the primary dispute resolution mechanism — a quick and relatively inexpensive process that produces a binding but temporarily enforceable decision.

Adjudication under the HGCRA

The Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 gives parties to a construction contract the right to refer disputes to adjudication at any time. The adjudication process must be completed within 28 days of referral (extendable to 42 days with the referring party's consent). The adjudicator's decision is binding and must be complied with immediately — it can only be challenged in subsequent arbitration or litigation. Building surveying candidates must understand the adjudication process, the types of dispute that are commonly referred, and the practical implications of an adjudication for an ongoing construction project.

Party wall disputes

The Party Wall etc. Act 1996 provides a statutory framework for resolving party wall disputes — but disputes still arise, most commonly over the schedule of condition, the scope of works permitted under the Act, and the assessment of damage following completion of works. Where the appointed surveyors cannot agree an award, a third surveyor is appointed to make the determination. Party wall surveyors must maintain their professional independence — they are not advocates for the party who appointed them, they are independent surveyors whose duty is to make a fair award. Candidates acting as party wall surveyors must understand the third surveyor process and the criteria for challenging an award in the county court.

Defect and negligence disputes

Building survey reports are a significant source of professional negligence claims. A surveyor who fails to identify a significant defect in a building survey report may face a claim from the client for the cost of remediation or the diminution in value of the property. The most effective risk management is a thorough and competent survey, a clear and comprehensive report, and written terms of engagement that define the scope and limitations of the service. When a complaint or claim arises respond promptly, notify your professional indemnity insurers immediately, and do not admit liability without taking legal advice.

RICS dispute resolution services

RICS DRS provides a range of dispute resolution services relevant to building surveying practice — adjudication, arbitration, mediation, and expert determination. Expert determination is particularly appropriate for technical disputes about building defects, the scope of contract works, or the valuation of variations where the parties want a quick and cost-effective resolution from someone with relevant technical expertise. Mediation is effective for disputes where the relationship between the parties — employer and contractor, building owner and adjoining owner — needs to be preserved for the long term.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of conflict avoidance principles in building surveying practice. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you managed a contract administration dispute, dealt with a party wall disagreement, responded to a defect complaint, or advised a client on dispute resolution options. Prepare examples that show professional judgement in managing conflict — not just a description of the available mechanisms.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Building Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 10 covered sustainability at a general level. Building surveying practice sits at the centre of the sustainability agenda for the built environment — the assessment, specification, and management of existing buildings offers the greatest opportunity to reduce the carbon footprint of the UK's building stock.

Retrofit and energy efficiency

The majority of the UK's existing building stock will still be standing in 2050 — which means that achieving net zero requires the deep retrofit of millions of existing buildings rather than simply building new low-carbon ones. Building surveyors are central to the retrofit agenda — assessing the energy performance of existing buildings, specifying retrofit measures, managing retrofit projects, and advising clients on the financial and technical implications of improvement works. Key retrofit measures include: external and internal wall insulation; roof and floor insulation; high-performance glazing; air tightness improvements; mechanical ventilation with heat recovery; and the replacement of fossil fuel heating systems with heat pumps. Understanding the specific challenges of retrofit — interstitial condensation risk, thermal bridging, heritage constraints, and the sequencing of measures — is essential for building surveying candidates advising on retrofit projects.

Energy Performance Certificates

EPCs provide a standardised assessment of a building's energy performance on a scale from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient). Understanding EPCs — what they measure, how they are produced, and what their limitations are — is essential for building surveying candidates. Minimum energy efficiency standards for private rented commercial property currently require a minimum EPC rating of E for new leases and lease renewals — the government has consulted on raising this to B by 2030. Advising clients on the EPC implications of their property decisions — acquisition, letting, refurbishment — is a routine building surveying instruction.

Building regulations and Part L

Part L of the Building Regulations sets the energy efficiency standards for new buildings and for certain works to existing buildings. Building surveyors advising on extensions, refurbishments, and change of use must understand the Part L requirements applicable to the works — what triggers a Part L assessment, what the minimum U-value standards are, and how to demonstrate compliance. The Future Buildings Standard is expected to significantly raise the energy efficiency requirements for new buildings and major refurbishments — candidates should be aware of the direction of travel even where the detailed requirements are still emerging.

Historic and heritage buildings

Improving the energy efficiency of historic and heritage buildings presents specific challenges — many standard retrofit measures are inappropriate or not permitted for listed buildings or buildings in conservation areas. Building surveyors working with the historic environment must understand the planning and listed building consent requirements for energy efficiency works, the alternative measures available for historic buildings, and the SPAB and Historic England guidance on sustainable retrofit of traditional buildings. The moisture performance of traditional building materials — solid brick and stone walls that breathe rather than resist moisture — is particularly important to understand when specifying insulation for historic buildings.

Sustainable drainage and water management

Building surveyors advising on new development and significant refurbishment must understand the sustainable drainage requirements — SUDS (sustainable urban drainage systems) are required for all new development in many local authority areas and may be required for refurbishment projects that significantly change the impermeable area of a site. Understanding the basic SUDS options — permeable paving, green roofs, attenuation tanks, swales — and their implications for design and maintenance is a relevant sustainability skill for building surveying candidates.

Embodied carbon

Embodied carbon — the carbon dioxide emitted in the manufacture, transport, and installation of building materials — is increasingly recognised as a significant contributor to the built environment's carbon footprint. Building surveyors specifying materials for new construction and refurbishment should understand the concept of embodied carbon, be aware of the tools available for measuring it (RICS Whole Life Carbon Assessment guidance, One Click LCA), and be able to advise clients on specification choices that reduce embodied carbon without compromising performance.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of sustainability principles in building surveying instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where sustainability considerations affected your advice — specifying retrofit measures, advising on EPC compliance, managing Part L requirements, or advising on historic building retrofit. Assessors will probe the depth of your sustainability knowledge — generic answers about the importance of sustainability will not satisfy a Building Surveying assessor who expects pathway-specific application.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
You have now covered the nine substantive areas of Building Surveying pathway preparation. Before you move to Module 12, use this section to practise Building Surveying APC scenarios with Michael — in both Tutor Mode and Assessor Mode.

How to use Michael for Building Surveying APC preparation

Michael has full Building Surveying pathway knowledge — building pathology and defect diagnosis, JCT contract suite, CDM Regulations 2015, Party Wall etc. Act 1996, planning and building regulations including the Building Safety Act 2022, asbestos regulations, fire safety, BCIS cost data, NBS specification, and the full range of Building Surveying technical content covered in your 50 pathway questions.

Use Tutor Mode to develop your understanding — ask Michael to explain the diagnosis of rising damp versus penetrating damp, walk you through the CDM dutyholder roles, help you structure a contract administration competency example, or clarify the extension of time assessment process under JCT SBC.

Use Assessor Mode to test your readiness — ask Michael to present a defect scenario and ask you to diagnose it, run a mock contract administration challenge, probe your knowledge of the Party Wall Act, or test your understanding of the Building Safety Act gateway process.

Suggested Building Surveying APC practice scenarios

  • Competency selection — Ask Michael to review your competency selection. Confirm your grouped optional choice and your full technical list optional, and ask him to challenge whether your selection is coherent and well-evidenced against your day-to-day work.
  • Building pathology — Ask Michael to present a defect scenario — dampness in a solid brick Victorian terraced house, cracking in a 1960s concrete framed office building, or roof spread in a traditional timber framed structure. Ask him to follow up on your diagnostic methodology, the investigation approach, and the remediation specification.
  • Contract administration — Ask Michael to run a mock contract administration session — a contractor has submitted an extension of time claim for 8 weeks citing exceptionally adverse weather and late information. Ask him to follow up on your assessment methodology, the relevant contract provisions, and how you would communicate your decision to both parties.
  • Party Wall — Ask Michael to present a party wall scenario — a building owner wants to carry out underpinning works within 3 metres of the adjoining owner's foundation. Ask him to follow up on the notice requirements, the schedule of condition process, and the award procedure.
  • CDM — Ask Michael to test your knowledge of the CDM dutyholder roles. Ask him to present a project scenario and ask you to identify the dutyholder appointments required, the F10 notification trigger, and the Health and Safety File obligations.
  • Sustainability — Ask Michael to present a retrofit scenario — a 1930s semi-detached house with solid brick walls, single glazing, and a gas boiler. The client wants to achieve an EPC rating of C. Ask him to follow up on the measures you would specify, the risks of interstitial condensation, and how you would sequence the works.
  • Building Safety Act — Ask Michael to test your knowledge of the Building Safety Act 2022. Ask him to present a higher-risk building project and ask you to identify the gateway requirements, the dutyholder roles, and the competency requirements for those involved.

Common Building Surveying referral patterns

  • Shallow building pathology knowledge — candidates who can describe defects but cannot diagnose the cause or explain the investigation methodology needed to confirm it.
  • Poor contract administration depth — candidates who know the JCT framework in general terms but cannot apply specific contract provisions under follow-up questioning — particularly extensions of time, loss and expense, and the payment notice regime.
  • Inadequate CDM knowledge — candidates who cannot explain the dutyholder roles, the F10 notification trigger, or the Health and Safety File requirements with confidence.
  • Outdated regulatory knowledge — candidates unaware of the Building Safety Act 2022 gateway process, the current Part L requirements, or recent changes to building regulations.
  • Generic sustainability answers — candidates who discuss sustainability in general terms without demonstrating pathway-specific application — energy efficiency in existing buildings, retrofit challenges, Part L compliance — is what Building Surveying assessors expect.

Review your performance against these common referral patterns. If any apply to you return to the relevant sections of Module 11B and use Michael to address the gap before moving to Module 12.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
This assessment tests your readiness to move from mandatory competency preparation into your final APC simulation in Module 12. It covers all nine substantive areas of Module 11B.

Work through the questions honestly. Where you find gaps return to the relevant section and use Michael in Tutor Mode to consolidate your understanding before attempting Module 12.

  1. Your competency selection includes Building pathology, Construction technology and environmental services, Contract administration, Design and specification, Inspection, and Legal and regulatory compliance all to Level 3, plus Fire safety to Level 1. A colleague suggests you should take Fire safety to Level 3 as an optional competency. What questions would you ask yourself before deciding whether to do so?
  2. You are about to carry out a full building survey of a 1980s commercial office building that has been vacant for two years. Describe your pre-survey risk assessment — what specific hazards would you consider and what precautions would you take before entering the building?
  3. A contractor on a JCT Standard Building Contract has submitted an interim valuation of £485,000. Your assessment of the value of work properly executed is £420,000. The contractor has also included £35,000 for materials on site that you have not been able to verify. How do you proceed and what certificate do you issue?
  4. A client asks you to explain the difference between a management survey and a refurbishment and demolition survey under the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012. What do you tell them, and what are the consequences of carrying out refurbishment works without an R&D survey on a pre-2000 building?
  5. You are acting as party wall surveyor for a building owner who wants to carry out a loft conversion involving raising the party wall by 600mm. The adjoining owner has dissented. Describe the party wall process from this point — what notices have been served, what happens next, and what will the award cover?
  6. A contractor on a JCT Intermediate Building Contract has submitted an extension of time claim for six weeks, citing late architect's instructions and exceptionally adverse weather. How do you assess the claim, what is the relevant contract clause, and what are the consequences of failing to grant a valid extension of time?
  7. A residential client asks you to advise on improving the energy efficiency of their 1930s semi-detached house with solid brick walls. They want to achieve an EPC rating of C. What measures would you consider, what are the key risks of each, and how would you sequence the works?
  8. You are advising a developer client on a proposed residential development of 25 units in a building that will be 22 metres in height. What are the Building Safety Act 2022 implications, what gateway approvals are required, and what dutyholder roles need to be appointed?
  9. A building owner client is unhappy with your interim certificate — they believe you have over-certified the contractor's claim for loss and expense and want you to issue a revised certificate reducing the amount. How do you respond?
  10. An assessor asks: "Tell me about the most technically challenging building defect you have investigated — what was the defect, how did you diagnose it, and what did you recommend?" What makes a high-scoring answer to this question and what are the most common referral mistakes candidates make?

Review your answers against the content in sections 11B.2 to 11B.9. For any question where you struggled return to the relevant section and use Michael in Assessor Mode to practise until you can answer confidently and with depth.

When you are satisfied with your performance across all ten questions you are ready for Module 12 — Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

sections.h: 11B.12 If You've Been Referred: What This Module Means for You
sections.body:
If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Building Surveying professional. It's specific, actionable feedback about what didn't land clearly enough in a particular interview, on a particular day, in front of a particular panel. Most successful resit candidates aren't relearning their pathway from scratch — they're closing specific gaps identified in their referral report.

How to use this module differently on a resit

  • Go back to your actual referral report before you start, and map its specific feedback points against the sections in this module — if your referral cited a gap in, for example, conflict avoidance or business planning, prioritise that section rather than working through everything in the original order
  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Building Surveying-specific material here

Referral rates on Building Surveying and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m11b.title: Quantity Surveying Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Pathway-specific preparation for Quantity Surveying and Construction candidates — professional practice, technical tools, and specialist knowledge for the APC final assessment.

sections.h: 11B.0 Understanding Your Technical Pathway Module
sections.body:
Before you work through the rest of Module 11B, it's worth understanding what this module actually is and why it sits where it does in your journey to Chartered status.

Modules 1 through 11 built your grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies — the ethics, client care, communication, health and safety, and business skills every RICS candidate needs, regardless of pathway. That knowledge is necessary, but it isn't sufficient on its own. Assessors don't just want to know that you understand client care in the abstract — they want to see you apply it specifically to the kind of work Quantity Surveying and Construction candidates actually do.

That's what this module is for. Everything from here through the end of Module 11B has been built and verified specifically against the current official RICS Quantity Surveying and Construction pathway guide — not a generic template with your pathway's name inserted. The competency structure, the legal and technical detail, and the Module 12 scenario at the end are all grounded in what Quantity Surveying and Construction candidates are genuinely tested on.

How to use this module well

  • Treat the competency structure section (11B.2) as your reference point when finalising your own declaration with your counsellor — it's a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it
  • Read every section with your own PDR experience in mind — the goal is connecting this material to what you've actually done, not memorising it in the abstract
  • Use Michael, your AI tutor, to pressure-test your answers on the scenarios that feel less familiar, not just the ones you're already confident on
  • Treat the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine practice interview question, not a reading exercise — actually formulate your answer before checking the model response

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain, in your own words, why Quantity Surveying and Construction candidates are tested the way they are — not just recite what the test covers.

sections.h: 11B.1 Introduction and Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
The Quantity Surveying and Construction pathway is one of the most commercially focused in the RICS portfolio. Quantity surveyors sit at the heart of the financial management of construction projects — from early cost advice and procurement through to contract administration, final account, and dispute resolution. The commercial acumen, contractual knowledge, and cost management skills expected of a chartered quantity surveyor are tested rigorously at APC assessment.

No other pathway requires the same depth of knowledge across procurement strategy, contract law, cost planning, and commercial management in a construction context. Quantity surveying candidates must be technically precise, commercially astute, and able to apply their knowledge under pressure across a wide range of project types and procurement routes.

This module bridges the gap between the mandatory competencies you covered in M01 to M11 and the specific knowledge, tools, and professional context of Quantity Surveying practice. By the time you complete M11B you will be ready for the technical question bank, the mock interview, and the APC assessment itself.

Michael has full Quantity Surveying pathway knowledge — the December 2025 RICS requirements, JCT and NEC contract suites, RICS New Rules of Measurement, cost planning methodology, procurement strategy, extension of time and loss and expense assessment, adjudication under the HGCRA, and current RICS guidance. Use him throughout this module and throughout your preparation.

Learning Outcomes

  • Explain the QS pathway competency structure and make informed competency selection decisions
  • Identify and manage health and safety risks specific to quantity surveying practice including CDM obligations
  • Apply accounting principles to construction cost management including cost plans, interim valuations, and final accounts
  • Use specialist QS data sources and professional tools accurately and confidently
  • Demonstrate client care skills appropriate to QS instructions across employer and contractor contexts
  • Manage construction contracts commercially and resolve disputes professionally
  • Identify and manage conflict in QS contexts including adjudication and final account disputes
  • Evidence sustainability competence through whole life cost advice and low-carbon construction
  • Practise QS APC scenarios with Michael in both Tutor Mode and Assessor Mode

sections.h: 11B.2 The Quantity Surveying Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
The Quantity Surveying and Construction pathway has a distinctive competency structure with a core competency that varies depending on your working environment — making it one of the few pathways where the core selection is context-dependent rather than fixed.

Mandatory competencies

Common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway: Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

The core competencies

  • Commercial management of construction — Level 3 (for candidates working in a commercial or contracting environment)
  • Design economics and cost planning — Level 3 (for candidates working in a consulting environment)
  • Construction technology and environmental services — Level 3
  • Contract practice — Level 3
  • Procurement and tendering — Level 3
  • Project finance — Level 3
  • Quantification and costing — Level 3

The commercial management versus design economics rule

This is the most important competency selection rule on the QS pathway. If you work primarily in a commercial or contracting environment — for a main contractor or specialist subcontractor — your core competency is Commercial management of construction to Level 3. If you work primarily in a consulting environment — for an employer's quantity surveyor, cost consultant, or project management firm — your core competency is Design economics and cost planning to Level 3. You cannot select both — the choice must reflect your actual working context. Assessors will probe the coherence between your core competency choice and the examples you provide throughout your submission.

No "one from full list" requirement

Unlike most other RICS pathways the QS and Construction pathway does not include the standard requirement to select one competency from the full technical competency list. Your optional selection is governed entirely by your core and optional competency lists as set out in the pathway guide. Candidates sometimes try to apply this rule when it does not exist for their pathway — Michael will correct this if it comes up.

Optional competency selection

QS candidates select two optional competencies to Level 2. The grouped optional rule requires choosing ONE from: Conflict avoidance OR Sustainability. Plus one further optional competency to Level 2 from the pathway optional list — there is no requirement to select from the broader full technical competency list on this pathway. Your optional choices should complement your core competency and reflect your day-to-day practice.

What assessors expect

QS assessors will probe your commercial and contractual knowledge in depth. They will present contract administration scenarios and ask you to apply specific contract provisions. They will test your cost planning methodology and your knowledge of procurement routes. They will ask about your experience of disputes — extensions of time, loss and expense, adjudication — and probe the depth of your contractual understanding. Precision and commercial confidence are the marks of a strong QS candidate.

Ask Michael

Use Michael in Tutor Mode to confirm your core competency choice reflects your working context, and to test your understanding of the Level 3 requirements for your chosen core competency before finalising your submission.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Quantity surveying involves working on construction sites, in contractor offices, and with construction project teams across all phases of a project. Health and safety obligations are significant — particularly CDM duties which directly affect the QS role.

CDM Regulations 2015 and the QS role

The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 impose specific duties on all those involved in construction projects. Quantity surveyors most commonly act as the client's adviser on CDM compliance, as part of the Principal Designer's team in a consulting role, or as a commercial manager within a Principal Contractor's organisation. In all these roles you have obligations under CDM — to cooperate with other dutyholders, to provide information relevant to health and safety, and to ensure your commercial and contractual advice does not inadvertently undermine health and safety management on the project. Understanding which projects require notification to the HSE (F10), what triggers the appointment of a Principal Designer and Principal Contractor, and what the pre-construction health and safety information must contain is essential for QS candidates advising on procurement and contract strategy.

Construction site visits

Quantity surveyors carry out site visits for measurement, valuation, and inspection purposes throughout the construction process. On every site visit: confirm you have received a site induction; wear appropriate PPE (hard hat, high-visibility vest, steel-capped boots as a minimum); follow site rules at all times; never enter excavations, trenches, or confined spaces without appropriate controls; be aware of moving plant and vehicles; and maintain a safe distance from working areas. Your role as QS does not exempt you from site safety obligations.

Measurement and inspection at height

QS measurement and inspection sometimes requires access to elevated areas — scaffolding, work platforms, roof structures, and plant areas. Apply the Work at Height Regulations 2005 whenever working at height is required. Never access scaffolding that has not been inspected and tagged, and never work at height alone on a construction site.

Office and project environment risks

Much of the QS role is office-based — but project office environments on large construction sites carry their own risks including fire, manual handling of large document sets and samples, and display screen equipment. Ensure your workstation is set up correctly for extended use, take regular breaks from screen-based work, and follow fire evacuation procedures for temporary site office accommodation.

Lone working and remote sites

QS measurement and valuation work sometimes involves visiting remote or partly constructed sites alone. Before any lone site visit ensure a colleague knows your location and expected return time, carry a fully charged mobile phone, and confirm the site contact details in case of emergency.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of health and safety knowledge in QS practice. Your competency examples should include specific instances where CDM obligations affected your advice or your conduct on a project — not generic descriptions of health and safety awareness. Assessors will probe your CDM knowledge in particular — know your duties and be prepared to give specific examples from your experience.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 6 covered accounting principles at a general level. For QS candidates accounting principles are a core competency area — the financial management of construction contracts requires a thorough understanding of cost planning, interim valuations, variations, loss and expense, and final accounts.

Cost planning and cost management

A cost plan is the QS's primary tool for managing the client's budget throughout the design and construction process. Cost plans are prepared at progressively greater levels of detail as the design develops — from an initial order of magnitude estimate at feasibility stage through to a detailed elemental cost plan at tender stage. Each cost plan must be clearly based on the assumptions made at that stage of design — assumptions about specification, procurement route, programme, and market conditions — and must be updated as those assumptions change. The RICS New Rules of Measurement (NRM1) provides the standard framework for order of cost estimating and cost planning in the UK.

Interim valuations and payment

Under JCT contracts interim payments are made to the contractor based on the QS's valuation of work properly executed, materials on site, and other contract sums due. The payment regime under the Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 (as amended by the Local Democracy Economic Development and Construction Act 2009) requires the paying party to issue a payment notice within five days of the due date and a pay less notice at least five days before the final date for payment. Failure to issue these notices on time can result in the contractor's application becoming the sum due — a common source of disputes on poorly administered contracts. QS candidates must understand the payment notice regime thoroughly and be able to apply it under examination conditions.

Variations and change management

Variations are changes to the scope of the contract works instructed by the employer or contract administrator. Valuing variations requires understanding the contract valuation rules — using bill rates where applicable, fair rates where bill rates are not applicable, and daywork as a last resort. The cumulative financial impact of multiple variations — particularly on preliminaries and on the contractor's programme — is a common source of dispute and must be carefully tracked throughout the project. QS candidates must understand the difference between a variation and a contractor's claim — not every additional cost the contractor identifies is a variation under the contract.

Loss and expense

Direct loss and expense arises where the regular progress of the works has been materially affected by relevant matters — typically employer actions or inactions such as late information, variations, delayed access, or suspension of the works. Assessing loss and expense requires understanding the heads of claim — extended preliminaries, plant standing time, loss of productivity, subcontractor claims, head office overheads, and financing charges — and the evidence required to support each head. Many loss and expense claims are poorly substantiated — the QS must assess each head on the evidence provided and not simply accept or reject the claim in total.

Final accounts

The final account settles the total amount due under the contract — incorporating all variations, loss and expense, fluctuations, and other adjustments. Preparing or agreeing a final account on a complex project is one of the most technically demanding tasks in QS practice, requiring a thorough understanding of the contract, a complete record of all variations and instructions, and the ability to assess and negotiate contractor claims fairly and commercially.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of accounting principles in QS instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you prepared a cost plan, assessed an interim valuation, managed variations, assessed a loss and expense claim, or contributed to a final account. Assessors will probe your understanding of the HGCRA payment regime, the NRM cost planning framework, and the principles of loss and expense assessment in particular.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
QS practice relies on a specific set of data sources and professional tools. Competent use of these tools is expected at APC Level 2 — assessors will ask which sources you used in specific instructions and why.

RICS New Rules of Measurement

The NRM suite provides the standard framework for measurement and cost management in the UK. NRM1 covers order of cost estimating and cost planning. NRM2 covers detailed measurement for building works — the standard method of measurement used for preparing bills of quantities. NRM3 covers maintenance cost planning and life cycle costing. QS candidates must be familiar with all three volumes and understand when each is applicable. The ability to apply NRM correctly in cost planning and measurement is a fundamental QS skill that assessors will test.

BCIS — Building Cost Information Service

BCIS provides construction cost data including elemental cost analyses, tender price indices, and location factors. QS candidates use BCIS data to benchmark cost plans, prepare order of cost estimates, and validate tender returns. Understanding the limitations of BCIS data — the importance of adjusting for location, specification, contract size, and current market conditions — is as important as knowing how to access it.

JCT contract suite

The Joint Contracts Tribunal publishes the standard forms of building contract most widely used in the UK. QS candidates must be familiar with JCT SBC (Standard Building Contract), JCT IBC (Intermediate Building Contract), JCT MW (Minor Works), JCT DB (Design and Build), and JCT MTC (Measured Term Contract). Each form has specific provisions for payment, variations, extensions of time, loss and expense, and dispute resolution that the QS must understand and apply correctly.

NEC contract suite

The NEC (New Engineering Contract) suite is increasingly used on public sector and infrastructure projects. The NEC4 Engineering and Construction Contract (ECC) is the main form — its compensation event mechanism differs fundamentally from the JCT variation and loss and expense regime and requires a different approach to commercial management. QS candidates working in sectors where NEC is prevalent must understand the compensation event process, the early warning notice system, and the programme management obligations of the NEC.

BIM and digital tools

Building Information Modelling is increasingly used on construction projects and directly affects the QS role — model-based quantity take-off, 5D BIM (cost integrated with the model), and digital collaboration platforms change how QS measurement and cost management is carried out. QS candidates should be familiar with BIM Level 2 requirements, the common data environment, and the tools used in their firm's practice. The RICS guidance on BIM and the QS role is a relevant reference document.

Specialist QS software

QS practice uses specialist software for measurement, cost planning, and contract administration — including CostX, Causeway, Procore, and various cost management platforms. Candidates should be familiar with the tools used in their firm and be able to explain how they support the accuracy and efficiency of QS work.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate that you use appropriate data sources and tools in your professional work. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you applied NRM, used BCIS data, worked with a JCT or NEC contract, or used specialist QS software to manage cost or contract information. Be precise about which tools you used and explain why they were relevant to the specific instruction.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 3 covered client care at a general level. QS practice involves acting for a range of clients — employers, contractors, subcontractors, and funders — and the client care considerations differ significantly depending on which side of the contract you are working on.

Acting for the employer

When acting as employer's QS or cost consultant your primary duty is to the employer client — providing accurate cost advice, managing the budget, administering the contract fairly, and protecting the employer's commercial interests. Managing employer expectations on cost is one of the most challenging client care tasks in QS practice — clients frequently have budget expectations that are not achievable at the specified quality and programme. Providing honest and timely cost advice — even when it is unwelcome — is a professional obligation. Document all cost advice clearly and ensure the client understands the assumptions and risks behind every estimate.

Acting for the contractor

When acting as commercial manager for a main contractor or specialist subcontractor your duty is to protect and maximise the contractor's commercial position — identifying and pursuing legitimate claims, managing subcontractor accounts, and ensuring the contractor's contractual entitlements are properly documented and pursued. This role requires commercial assertiveness alongside professional integrity — pursuing claims that are not contractually supported, or withholding payments from subcontractors without proper basis, creates professional and legal risk.

Managing the contract administrator relationship

When acting as employer's QS alongside a separate contract administrator (architect or project manager) clarity about respective roles is essential. The QS's role in interim valuations, variation valuation, and final account preparation must be clearly defined and agreed at the outset. Disputes between employer's QS and contract administrator about their respective roles and responsibilities are a common source of project problems — clear written terms of appointment and regular communication between the professional team are the most effective preventive measures.

Multi-disciplinary project teams

Large construction projects involve multiple professional advisers — architects, engineers, project managers, planning consultants, and specialist advisers alongside the QS. Managing relationships within the professional team, communicating cost information clearly to non-QS professionals, and ensuring that design decisions are made with full awareness of their cost implications requires strong interpersonal and communication skills alongside technical QS expertise.

Conflicts of interest

QS practitioners sometimes face conflicts of interest — acting for both employer and contractor on a project, or acting for a client where another part of the firm has a conflicting commercial interest. RICS Rules of Conduct require identification and management of conflicts before accepting instructions. In QS practice, the most common conflict scenario is acting as adjudicator or expert witness on a dispute involving a party with whom the firm has an existing professional relationship — rigorous conflict checking before accepting any dispute-related appointment is essential.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of client care principles in QS instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you managed client expectations on cost, adapted your approach to acting for employer versus contractor, managed relationships within a professional team, or identified and managed a conflict of interest. Prepare examples that show genuine professional judgement in managing complex client relationships.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 7 covered business planning at a general level. For QS candidates business planning encompasses both the strategic cost and procurement advice given to clients and the commercial management of the QS's own practice and fee income.

Procurement strategy advice

Advising clients on procurement strategy — how to organise the design and construction process to achieve their objectives — is a core QS business planning skill. The main procurement routes include: traditional (design then tender then build, with a contract administrator); design and build (contractor takes design and construction responsibility); management contracting; and construction management. Each route has different implications for cost certainty, programme, risk allocation, and client involvement. QS candidates must be able to explain the key features of each procurement route, advise on the most appropriate approach for a specific client and project, and understand the contractual framework best suited to each route.

Tender strategy and market engagement

Advising on tender strategy — open tender, selective tender, negotiated tender, or two-stage tender — is a QS advisory skill that directly affects the quality and competitiveness of tenders received. Two-stage tendering is increasingly common on complex projects — the first stage selects a preferred contractor based on preliminaries and overheads, and the second stage develops the detailed price with the preferred contractor using open book pricing. QS candidates must understand the advantages and risks of each approach and be able to advise clients on the tender strategy most likely to achieve value for money in current market conditions.

Value engineering

Value engineering is the systematic review of design and specification decisions to identify opportunities to achieve the required function at lower cost without compromising quality. QS candidates must be able to facilitate value engineering workshops, identify and evaluate value engineering opportunities, and present the results to clients and design teams. Value engineering is most effective early in the design process — value engineering at tender stage or on site is significantly less effective and more disruptive than early design-stage intervention.

Whole life costing

Whole life costing assesses the total cost of a building over its full life cycle — including capital cost, maintenance and operating costs, and end-of-life costs — rather than focusing solely on the initial construction cost. Advising clients to make design and specification decisions on a whole life cost basis — rather than minimising initial capital cost — is increasingly expected of QS practitioners, particularly on public sector projects where whole life value is a procurement requirement. The RICS guidance on whole life costing and the NRM3 framework for maintenance cost planning are the key reference documents.

Commercial management and cash flow

On contractor-side QS practice commercial management includes managing the project's cash flow — ensuring interim applications are submitted on time and in sufficient detail, pursuing outstanding payments promptly, and managing subcontractor payments in accordance with the contract and the Construction Act. Cash flow is the lifeblood of a construction business — poor cash flow management is one of the most common causes of contractor insolvency. QS candidates working in commercial management must understand the project's cash flow position at all times and take proactive steps to protect it.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of business planning principles in QS instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you advised on procurement strategy, contributed to a value engineering exercise, prepared a whole life cost analysis, or managed a project's commercial cash flow position. Assessors will look for evidence that you understand the strategic and commercial dimensions of construction projects, not just the technical measurement aspects.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 8 covered conflict avoidance at a general level. Construction contracts are a fertile source of disputes — and QS practitioners are at the centre of most of them. Understanding how to avoid disputes and how to manage them when they arise is a core professional skill.

Extension of time disputes

Extension of time disputes are among the most common in construction — arising where the contractor claims additional time due to employer-caused delays or other relevant events under the contract. Under JCT SBC the contract administrator must assess EOT claims against the relevant events listed in the contract (clause 2.29), consider only the delay caused by those events, and grant a fair and reasonable extension where entitlement exists. Failure to grant a valid EOT can have serious consequences — time at large, loss of the employer's right to deduct liquidated damages, and potential claims for additional loss and expense. QS candidates acting as contract administrator or commercial adviser must understand the EOT assessment methodology thoroughly and apply it consistently and promptly.

Loss and expense disputes

Loss and expense disputes arise when the contractor claims financial compensation for delays and disruptions caused by relevant matters under the contract. These disputes are often protracted and expensive because the contractor's evidence of actual loss is frequently inadequate and the quantum of the claim is difficult to verify independently. QS candidates must understand the heads of claim, the evidence required to support each head, and the distinction between direct loss and expense (recoverable under the contract) and other costs that are not recoverable. Robust records — of programme, resources, costs, and correspondence — are the most effective way to manage loss and expense disputes on both sides of the contract.

Adjudication

The Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 gives parties to a construction contract the right to refer disputes to adjudication at any time. Adjudication is fast (28 days from referral to decision), relatively inexpensive, and produces a binding decision that must be complied with immediately. QS candidates must understand the adjudication process, the types of dispute commonly referred (payment disputes, EOT disputes, variation valuation disputes, final account disputes), and the practical implications of an adjudication for an ongoing construction project. Many QS practitioners either manage adjudications directly or support specialist legal teams — understanding the process and the evidence required is essential.

Subcontractor disputes

Main contractor QS practitioners regularly deal with subcontractor disputes — over payment, variations, extensions of time, and final accounts. The Construction Act payment provisions apply equally to subcontracts as to main contracts — subcontractors have the same right to adjudicate as main contractors. Managing subcontractor commercial relationships professionally — paying what is properly due on time, assessing variations fairly, and resolving disputes promptly — is both a legal obligation and a practical necessity for maintaining the project supply chain.

Preventing disputes through documentation

The most effective conflict avoidance tool in QS practice is rigorous documentation. Every instruction, variation, EOT claim, and loss and expense notification must be recorded in writing, responded to promptly, and filed completely. A well-maintained commercial file is the QS's primary defence in any dispute. QS candidates must develop the habit of contemporaneous record-keeping — records made at the time are far more credible in adjudication or arbitration than records reconstructed after a dispute has arisen.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of conflict avoidance principles in QS instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where you assessed an EOT claim, managed a loss and expense dispute, supported or managed an adjudication, or resolved a subcontractor commercial dispute. Prepare examples that show professional judgement in managing commercial conflict — not just a description of the available dispute resolution mechanisms.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Quantity Surveying Practice
sections.body:
Module 10 covered sustainability at a general level. QS practice has a specific and important relationship with sustainability — the QS's role in cost planning, procurement, and contract management directly affects the sustainability outcomes of construction projects.

Whole life carbon assessment

The RICS Whole Life Carbon Assessment Professional Statement (2023) sets out mandatory requirements for RICS members carrying out whole life carbon assessments on buildings. Whole life carbon encompasses both embodied carbon (the carbon emitted in manufacturing, transporting, and installing building materials) and operational carbon (the carbon emitted in heating, cooling, and powering the building over its lifetime). QS candidates must understand the RICS WLCA framework, the tools used for embodied carbon assessment (One Click LCA, EC3), and how whole life carbon considerations are incorporated into procurement and design decisions. The 2025 RICS update to the WLCA Professional Statement is the current reference document.

Sustainable procurement

Procurement strategy has a direct impact on the sustainability of construction projects — through supply chain selection, contract requirements, and the environmental standards embedded in the specification. QS practitioners advising on procurement can embed sustainability requirements throughout the process: pre-qualification criteria that assess contractors' environmental management systems and carbon reduction plans; tender evaluation criteria that weight sustainability performance alongside price; and contract provisions that require reporting on embodied carbon, waste management, and supply chain practices. Understanding how to embed sustainability in procurement without creating unenforceable contract obligations is a practical QS skill.

Modern Methods of Construction

Modern Methods of Construction — including volumetric modular construction, panelised systems, and structural insulated panels — offer significant sustainability benefits compared to traditional construction: reduced waste on site, improved quality control, shorter programme, and lower embodied carbon in some applications. QS candidates should understand the cost planning implications of MMC — the cost profile is different from traditional construction, with higher manufacturing costs offset by reduced on-site labour and programme savings — and be able to advise clients on the whole life cost implications of MMC versus traditional procurement.

Waste management and the circular economy

Construction and demolition waste is one of the largest waste streams in the UK. QS practitioners can influence waste outcomes through specification — specifying materials with high recycled content, designing for disassembly, and requiring waste management plans from contractors. The Site Waste Management Plans Regulations (now incorporated into best practice guidance) and the contractor's obligations under the waste hierarchy are relevant to QS candidates advising on contract requirements and monitoring contractor performance.

Social value

Social value — the broader social, economic, and environmental benefits generated by construction procurement — is increasingly required in public sector procurement under the Social Value Act 2012 and the associated policy note PPN 06/20. QS candidates involved in public sector procurement must understand how to incorporate social value requirements into tender evaluation, how to specify and measure social value commitments, and how to monitor delivery against those commitments throughout the project.

APC Level 2 application

At Level 2 you are expected to demonstrate practical application of sustainability principles in QS instructions. Your competency examples should include specific instances where sustainability considerations affected your cost planning, procurement advice, or contract management — whole life carbon assessment, sustainable procurement criteria, MMC cost planning, or social value measurement. Assessors will probe the depth of your sustainability knowledge — generic answers about the importance of sustainability will not satisfy a QS assessor who expects pathway-specific application.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
You have now covered the nine substantive areas of Quantity Surveying pathway preparation. Before you move to Module 12, use this section to practise QS APC scenarios with Michael — in both Tutor Mode and Assessor Mode.

How to use Michael for QS APC preparation

Michael has full Quantity Surveying pathway knowledge — the NRM suite, BCIS cost data, JCT and NEC contract suites, the HGCRA payment regime, extension of time and loss and expense assessment, adjudication procedure, CDM obligations, whole life carbon assessment, sustainable procurement, and the commercial management versus design economics core competency rule.

Use Tutor Mode to develop your understanding — ask Michael to explain the NRM1 cost planning framework, walk you through the HGCRA payment notice regime, help you structure a contract administration competency example, or clarify the compensation event mechanism under NEC4.

Use Assessor Mode to test your readiness — ask Michael to present a cost plan challenge, run a mock EOT assessment, probe your knowledge of the HGCRA payment provisions, or test your understanding of the adjudication process.

Suggested QS APC practice scenarios

  • Core competency selection — Ask Michael to confirm whether your working context means your core competency should be Commercial management of construction or Design economics and cost planning. Describe your day-to-day work and ask him to challenge whether your selection is correct and well-evidenced.
  • Cost planning — Ask Michael to present a cost planning scenario — a client has a budget of £4.5 million for a commercial office refurbishment and wants to know whether it is achievable. Ask him to follow up on your methodology, the BCIS data you would use, the assumptions you would make, and how you would present your advice.
  • Payment — Ask Michael to test your knowledge of the HGCRA payment regime. Present a scenario where the employer has failed to issue a payment notice. Ask him to follow up on the consequences, the contractor's options, and the pay less notice requirements.
  • Extension of time — Ask Michael to present an EOT scenario — a contractor has submitted a claim for 12 weeks delay citing late information and exceptionally adverse weather. Ask him to follow up on your assessment methodology, the relevant JCT clause, the evidence you would need, and how you would communicate your decision.
  • Loss and expense — Ask Michael to present a loss and expense scenario — a contractor claims £380,000 for extended preliminaries and loss of productivity following a prolonged suspension of the works. Ask him to follow up on the heads of claim, the evidence required, and how you would approach the assessment.
  • Adjudication — Ask Michael to present an adjudication scenario — a subcontractor has referred a payment dispute to adjudication. Ask him to follow up on the adjudication process, the timeframes, your role in supporting the responding party's case, and the enforcement of the decision.
  • Sustainability — Ask Michael to test your knowledge of the RICS Whole Life Carbon Assessment framework. Ask him to follow up on the difference between embodied and operational carbon, the tools available for embodied carbon measurement, and how WLCA requirements are incorporated into procurement.

Common QS referral patterns

  • Shallow contractual knowledge — candidates who describe the contract framework in general terms but cannot apply specific provisions under follow-up questioning — particularly the HGCRA payment regime, EOT assessment methodology, and loss and expense heads of claim.
  • Wrong core competency choice — candidates whose core competency choice (Commercial management versus Design economics) does not match the examples they provide in their submission, creating an incoherence that assessors identify immediately.
  • Poor NRM knowledge — candidates who reference NRM without being able to explain which volume applies to their instruction or how the measurement rules affect their cost plan or bill of quantities.
  • Inadequate dispute resolution depth — candidates who know adjudication exists but cannot explain the process, the timeframes, or the practical implications for an ongoing project.
  • Generic sustainability answers — candidates who discuss sustainability in general terms without demonstrating QS-specific application — whole life carbon, sustainable procurement, MMC cost planning — which is what QS assessors expect.

Review your performance against these common referral patterns. If any apply to you return to the relevant sections of Module 11B and use Michael to address the gap before moving to Module 12.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
This assessment tests your readiness to move from mandatory competency preparation into your final APC simulation in Module 12. It covers all nine substantive areas of Module 11B.

Work through the questions honestly. Where you find gaps return to the relevant section and use Michael in Tutor Mode to consolidate your understanding before attempting Module 12.

  1. You work as a QS in a consulting practice advising employer clients on cost management. A colleague who works for a main contractor tells you that your core competency should be Commercial management of construction because it is the more commercially focused option. How do you respond and why?
  2. You are about to carry out a measurement survey on a partially completed construction site to prepare an interim valuation. Describe your approach to health and safety before and during the site visit — what specific risks would you assess and what precautions would you take?
  3. A contractor on a JCT Standard Building Contract has submitted an interim application for £620,000. Your assessment of the value of work properly executed and materials on site is £540,000. The due date for payment is in three days. What notices must be issued, by whom, and by when — and what are the consequences of failing to issue them?
  4. A contractor has submitted an extension of time claim for ten weeks citing three causes of delay: exceptionally adverse weather (three weeks), late issue of architect's instructions (five weeks), and a subcontractor insolvency (two weeks). How do you assess each element and what extension would you grant?
  5. You are advising an employer client on the procurement strategy for a £8 million commercial office fit-out. The client wants price certainty, a fixed completion date, and minimal involvement in the design process. What procurement route would you recommend and why?
  6. A contractor is claiming £290,000 in loss and expense for extended preliminaries and head office overheads following a six-week suspension of the works instructed by the employer. What heads of claim would you assess, what evidence would you require for each, and how would you approach the negotiation of the final figure?
  7. You are preparing a cost plan for a new office building at RIBA Stage 2. The client's budget is £12 million. Describe your methodology — what data sources would you use, how would you structure the elemental cost plan, and how would you present your cost advice to the client?
  8. A subcontractor has referred a payment dispute to adjudication claiming £85,000 for unpaid variations. You are acting for the main contractor as responding party. Describe the adjudication process from referral to decision, your role in preparing the response, and the consequences if the decision goes against your client.
  9. A client asks you to advise on incorporating sustainability requirements into the procurement of a new commercial building. How would you embed whole life carbon, social value, and modern methods of construction into the tender process?
  10. An assessor asks: "Tell me about the most commercially challenging construction contract you have worked on — what made it challenging and how did you manage it?" What makes a high-scoring answer to this question and what are the most common referral mistakes QS candidates make?

Review your answers against the content in sections 11B.2 to 11B.9. For any question where you struggled return to the relevant section and use Michael in Assessor Mode to practise until you can answer confidently and with depth.

When you are satisfied with your performance across all ten questions you are ready for Module 12 — Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

sections.h: 11B.12 If You've Been Referred: What This Module Means for You
sections.body:
If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Quantity Surveying and Construction professional. It's specific, actionable feedback about what didn't land clearly enough in a particular interview, on a particular day, in front of a particular panel. Most successful resit candidates aren't relearning their pathway from scratch — they're closing specific gaps identified in their referral report.

How to use this module differently on a resit

  • Go back to your actual referral report before you start, and map its specific feedback points against the sections in this module — if your referral cited a gap in, for example, conflict avoidance or business planning, prioritise that section rather than working through everything in the original order
  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Quantity Surveying and Construction-specific material here

Referral rates on Quantity Surveying and Construction and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m11b.title: Commercial Real Estate Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Pathway-specific preparation for Commercial Real Estate candidates — professional practice, technical tools, and specialist knowledge for the APC final assessment.

sections.h: 11B.0 Understanding Your Technical Pathway Module
sections.body:
Before you work through the rest of Module 11B, it's worth understanding what this module actually is and why it sits where it does in your journey to Chartered status.

Modules 1 through 11 built your grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies — the ethics, client care, communication, health and safety, and business skills every RICS candidate needs, regardless of pathway. That knowledge is necessary, but it isn't sufficient on its own. Assessors don't just want to know that you understand client care in the abstract — they want to see you apply it specifically to the kind of work Commercial Real Estate candidates actually do.

That's what this module is for. Everything from here through the end of Module 11B has been built and verified specifically against the current official RICS Commercial Real Estate pathway guide — not a generic template with your pathway's name inserted. The competency structure, the legal and technical detail, and the Module 12 scenario at the end are all grounded in what Commercial Real Estate candidates are genuinely tested on.

How to use this module well

  • Treat the competency structure section (11B.2) as your reference point when finalising your own declaration with your counsellor — it's a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it
  • Read every section with your own PDR experience in mind — the goal is connecting this material to what you've actually done, not memorising it in the abstract
  • Use Michael, your AI tutor, to pressure-test your answers on the scenarios that feel less familiar, not just the ones you're already confident on
  • Treat the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine practice interview question, not a reading exercise — actually formulate your answer before checking the model response

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain, in your own words, why Commercial Real Estate candidates are tested the way they are — not just recite what the test covers.

sections.h: 11B.1 Introduction and Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
Welcome to Module 11B — your final period of structured learning before Module 12's revision and mock APC simulation. This module exists because technical competence in Commercial Real Estate is only half of what RICS assesses at final assessment. The other half is professional practice: how you conduct yourself, manage risk, communicate with clients, run a viable business, and operate ethically and sustainably within the profession.

Commercial Real Estate surveyors sit at the centre of some of the highest-value, highest-scrutiny transactions in the built environment — landlord and tenant negotiations, investment disposals, leasing campaigns, corporate portfolio decisions.
