Assessors expect candidates on this pathway to demonstrate not just technical fluency in valuation, leasing, and asset management, but the judgement, professionalism, and commercial awareness that a client would expect from someone about to be entrusted with significant financial decisions on their behalf.

Learning Outcomes

  • Explain the structure of the Commercial Real Estate pathway and justify your competency selections
  • Apply health and safety principles specific to commercial property inspections and management
  • Demonstrate working knowledge of accounting principles as they apply to CRE practice
  • Identify and use the data sources and professional tools relied on by CRE practitioners
  • Apply RICS client care standards to commercial real estate client relationships
  • Explain how a CRE consultancy or in-house team plans and sustains a viable business
  • Apply conflict avoidance and dispute resolution principles to landlord and tenant and transactional scenarios
  • Discuss sustainability considerations specific to commercial real estate
  • Practise applying this knowledge to realistic APC scenarios with Michael, your AI tutor
  • Demonstrate readiness through a full module assessment

This module assumes you have already worked through Modules 1–10 and hold a solid grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies. What follows sharpens that knowledge specifically for Commercial Real Estate practice.

sections.h: 11B.2 The Commercial Real Estate Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
The Commercial Real Estate pathway is built around the day-to-day reality of advising on and managing commercial property — offices, retail, industrial and leisure assets — on behalf of landlords, tenants, investors, and occupiers. Your work might span purchase, sale and leasing, property and asset management, landlord and tenant relationships, valuation, investment advice, and development appraisals.

Mandatory competencies

Common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway: Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

Core Commercial Real Estate competencies

All three required:

  • Inspection (Level 3)
  • Measurement (Level 2)
  • Valuation (Level 2)

Optional competencies

You select three optionals to Level 3, chosen from the CRE optional list of around 21 items. The first entry on that list is a grouped choice: Accounting principles and procedures, Conflict avoidance management and dispute resolution, Data management, or Sustainability. This is a ceiling rule — if you select from this group you can choose at most one, but you are not required to select from it at all. All three optional slots can be filled from the rest of the list. The remaining optional items are: Auctioneering, BIM management, Building pathology, Capital taxation, Compulsory purchase and compensation, Contaminated land, Corporate recovery and insolvency, Development appraisals, Insurance, Indirect investment vehicles, Investment management, Landlord and tenant, Leasing and letting, Legal/regulatory compliance, Loan security valuation, Local taxation/assessment, Planning and development management, Property finance and funding, Property management, Purchase and sale, and Strategic real estate consultancy.

In addition to your three optionals, you must select one further competency to Level 3, or two to Level 2, from the full list of technical competencies — the broader master list spanning all RICS pathways, set out in the Requirements and Competencies guide. This is a distinct list, not a recycled pick from CRE's own core or optional lists.

In practice, Landlord and tenant and Leasing and letting are among the most commonly selected optionals given how central they are to CRE day-to-day work — but they are not automatic. Your actual selection should be driven entirely by what you do in your own role, agreed with your counsellor.

Source: RICS Commercial Real Estate Pathway Guide (published 1 December 2025, amended January 2026) — always check your specific declaration against the current guide on the RICS website before finalising it with your counsellor, since RICS updates these periodically.

Assessors mark candidates against the level of competency claimed (Level 1: knowledge and understanding; Level 2: application of knowledge; Level 3: reasoned advice). For CRE candidates at Level 3, this means being able to advise a client on a landlord and tenant negotiation or a leasing strategy with the same confidence and judgement you'd expect from a senior colleague — not simply describing what the process involves.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
Commercial property work carries distinct health and safety exposure that differs from residential or rural practice — multi-let buildings, live construction sites during refit or fit-out, plant rooms, roof access, and lone working in vacant units.

Key legal framework

  • Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 — the foundation duty of care for employers and the self-employed
  • Construction (Design and Management) Regulations (CDM) — relevant where inspections coincide with fit-out or refurbishment works
  • Control of Asbestos Regulations — critical in older commercial stock; always check the asbestos register before inspecting pre-2000 buildings
  • Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order — relevant to multi-let and mixed-use commercial buildings

Practical application for CRE surveyors

Before any inspection, a competent CRE practitioner will check the building's fire risk assessment and asbestos register, confirm lone-working protocols with their firm, and assess site-specific risks (vacant unit security, live building services, roof or plant access). On multi-let buildings, coordination with managing agents and other occupiers is essential — you are rarely the only person with a legitimate interest in the building on any given day.

Lone working is a live risk in CRE practice, particularly when inspecting vacant units or attending sites outside normal hours for landlord and tenant matters. A properly briefed lone-working policy — check-in protocols, shared location tracking, and a clear escalation route — is not optional professional good practice; RICS expects candidates to demonstrate they understand and apply it.

At Level 3, you should be able to explain how you would identify, assess, and mitigate a specific health and safety risk you've encountered in your own CRE work — not recite the regulations in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
Every RICS member needs a working grasp of accounting principles, and Commercial Real Estate practice brings that knowledge into sharp, transaction-relevant focus.

Core areas relevant to CRE candidates

  • Client money handling — RICS Client Money Protection scheme requirements, particularly relevant where you handle rent collection, service charge funds, or deposits on behalf of landlords
  • Service charge accounting — understanding of the RICS Service Charges in Commercial Property Professional Statement, reconciliation processes, and the difference between recoverable and irrecoverable costs
  • Business accounts — reading a client's balance sheet and profit and loss account well enough to assess covenant strength in a landlord and tenant or leasing context
  • VAT on commercial property — the option to tax, and its practical implications for landlords, tenants, and transaction structuring

Practical application

A CRE surveyor advising a landlord on a new letting needs to be able to assess a prospective tenant's covenant strength — not perform a full credit analysis, but read the headline indicators (turnover trends, net current assets, any qualification in the auditor's report) and know when to recommend a formal credit check or additional security such as a rent deposit or guarantor.

Service charge accounting is a frequent source of landlord and tenant dispute. Understanding what is and isn't recoverable, how apportionment works across a multi-let building, and the reconciliation timeline expected by the RICS Professional Statement will come up repeatedly in both technical questions and case study discussion.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
Commercial Real Estate practice is data-intensive. Assessors expect candidates to know not just that data exists, but which source is fit for which purpose, and its limitations.

Core data sources

  • HM Land Registry — title, ownership, and registered leases
  • VOA (Valuation Office Agency) — rating list and business rates data
  • CoStar / Radius Data Exchange — commercial market transactions, comparable evidence, vacancy and availability data
  • EGi (Estates Gazette Interactive) — market intelligence, planning applications, transaction news
  • RICS Red Book Global Standards — valuation methodology and reporting requirements
  • Local authority planning portals — planning history, Section 106 obligations, and permitted development rights relevant to a commercial asset
  • EPC register — energy performance data, increasingly central to both valuation and MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards) compliance

Practical application

When advising on rental value, a CRE surveyor should be able to explain why they selected particular comparables (location, use class, lease terms, condition) over others, and be transparent about the limitations of any single data source — CoStar transaction data, for example, doesn't always capture incentive packages (rent-free periods, fit-out contributions) that materially affect headline versus effective rent.

At Level 3, you're expected to weigh conflicting data and reach a reasoned, defensible position — not simply report what a database says.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
RICS client care standards apply to every pathway, but Commercial Real Estate work often involves sophisticated, repeat-instructing clients — institutional landlords, corporate occupiers, private equity investors — alongside first-time or occasional clients such as owner-occupiers or smaller landlords. Good client care means calibrating to both.

Core requirements

  • Clear terms of engagement, agreed and confirmed in writing before work begins
  • A complaints handling procedure that meets RICS requirements, and that you can explain to a client if asked
  • Transparent fee structures — particularly important in CRE, where fees may be percentage-based (e.g. on rent secured or investment value) and conflicts of interest around fee structure need to be actively managed
  • Regular, proactive communication — CRE instructions often run over months (a leasing campaign, an investment disposal), and clients expect updates without having to chase

Practical application

A common CRE scenario at interview: a landlord client is unhappy that a leasing campaign hasn't produced results as quickly as expected. Good client care here isn't reassurance for its own sake — it's transparent reporting on market conditions, a clear explanation of what's been tried, and a frank discussion of whether the asking terms need to be reviewed. Assessors want to see that you can have that difficult conversation professionally, not avoid it.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
Whether you work for a large firm, a boutique agency, or in-house, RICS expects every candidate to understand how their team or business sustains itself commercially.

Core areas

  • Fee income models specific to CRE — retainer fees, transactional/success fees (e.g. percentage of rent or capital value secured), and hourly/project fees for advisory work
  • Resourcing and capacity planning — particularly relevant in CRE, where instructions can be lumpy (a large leasing campaign or portfolio disposal absorbing significant team capacity)
  • Marketing and business development — how CRE practices win and retain instructions in a relationship-driven, competitive market
  • Risk management at the business level — professional indemnity insurance, conflict checking processes, and the commercial risk of fee structures tied to transaction outcomes

Practical application

Be ready to discuss, from your own experience, how your team resources a large instruction (for example, a multi-let leasing campaign) and how success fees are structured and justified to a client. Assessors are testing commercial awareness — do you understand the business you work in, not just the technical work you do within it.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
Commercial Real Estate work generates conflict as a matter of course — landlord and tenant relationships are inherently adversarial at points, and CRE surveyors are frequently the ones managing that friction before it escalates to formal dispute.

Core framework

  • RICS Conflict Avoidance, Management and Dispute Resolution Professional Statement
  • Early identification of dispute risk — rent review disagreements, dilapidations, service charge disputes, breaches of lease covenant
  • The dispute resolution ladder: negotiation → mediation → expert determination or arbitration (particularly common in rent review) → litigation as a last resort
  • Conflicts of interest specific to CRE — acting for both landlord and tenant (even on unrelated matters), or advising on a transaction where your firm has a competing instruction

Practical application

A frequent scenario: you're instructed by a landlord on a rent review, and the tenant is represented by another surveyor at the same firm on an unrelated matter. Assessors want you to identify this as a potential conflict, explain how you'd manage it (information barriers, disclosure, or declining one instruction if the conflict can't be adequately managed), and reference the relevant RICS guidance — not just say “we'd be careful.”

Dilapidations disputes are a classic CRE conflict scenario worth having a real example ready for — they combine technical building knowledge, lease interpretation, and negotiation skill, and assessors like this territory because it tests several competencies at once.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Commercial Real Estate Practice
sections.body:
Sustainability has moved from a peripheral consideration to a core commercial driver in Commercial Real Estate — affecting valuation, leasing demand, and regulatory compliance simultaneously.

Key areas

  • MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards) — the current requirement that commercial properties meet a minimum EPC rating to be lawfully let, and the trajectory of tightening standards
  • EPC ratings — their role in both regulatory compliance and increasingly in investment and occupier decision-making (“brown discount” on poorly rated assets)
  • Green leases — clauses addressing landlord and tenant collaboration on energy performance, data sharing, and alterations
  • Embodied carbon — increasingly a consideration in refurbishment-versus-redevelopment decisions, alongside operational carbon
  • ESG reporting pressure — particularly from institutional investors and corporate occupiers with their own net-zero commitments, which flows down into asset-level requirements

Practical application

Be ready to discuss how MEES affects a landlord's asset strategy for a sub-standard EPC-rated building — the options (upgrade, exempt, or accept it can't be re-let), the cost-benefit judgement involved, and how you'd advise a client through that decision. Sustainability questions at interview increasingly test commercial judgement (what does this mean for value and letting risk) rather than pure technical or regulatory recall.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
This section is your space to practise applying everything above to realistic APC-style scenarios, working through them with Michael, your AI tutor.

Michael can run you through scenario-based questions specific to Commercial Real Estate — a landlord and tenant negotiation, a rent review reference, a service charge dispute, a sustainability-driven asset decision — and probe your answers the way an assessor would: asking you to justify your reasoning, challenging your position, and pushing you past description into advice.

How to use this section effectively

  • Bring real examples from your own PDR wherever possible — Michael will help you structure and sharpen them, but the substance should be yours
  • Practise the “what would you advise” follow-up, not just “what happened” — assessors mark judgement, not narrative
  • Use Michael to stress-test weak points — if you're less confident on service charge accounting or conflict scenarios, spend deliberate time there rather than defaulting to your strongest area

Open a session with Michael now and work through at least three CRE-specific scenarios before moving to the module assessment.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
Complete the following ten questions to check your readiness for Module 12. These mirror the style and difficulty of real APC interview questions on the Commercial Real Estate pathway — read each one as if a panel member had just asked it, and answer as you would in the room.

  1. A prospective tenant's accounts show a qualified auditor's opinion and declining net current assets. How would you advise your landlord client, and what steps might you recommend before proceeding with the letting?
  2. Explain the difference between recoverable and irrecoverable service charge costs, and how you would handle a tenant's formal challenge to a service charge reconciliation.
  3. You discover your firm is instructed by both parties in a rent review, on unrelated matters. How do you identify and manage this conflict, with reference to RICS guidance?
  4. A commercial building you're instructed to let has an EPC rating of F. Explain the legal position under MEES and the options you would present to your landlord client.
  5. Outline the health and safety checks you would carry out before inspecting a vacant unit in a part-let commercial building, and explain why lone-working protocols matter in this context.
  6. A landlord is frustrated that a leasing campaign has not produced offers within the expected timeframe. How would you approach this conversation, consistent with RICS client care standards?
  7. Explain how a success-fee structure on a letting instruction might create a conflict of interest, and how you would manage it.
  8. Describe the dispute resolution options available in a rent review disagreement, and explain when you would recommend expert determination over arbitration.
  9. What data sources would you rely on to support a rental valuation opinion, and how would you address a limitation in that evidence if challenged by the other side?
  10. Explain how your team resources and prices a large, multi-let leasing campaign, and the commercial risks involved in that model.

Once you've worked through all ten and are satisfied with your answers — ideally after testing them against Michael's follow-up questions — you're ready for Module 12: Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

sections.h: 11B.12 If You've Been Referred: What This Module Means for You
sections.body:
If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Commercial Real Estate professional. It's specific, actionable feedback about what didn't land clearly enough in a particular interview, on a particular day, in front of a particular panel. Most successful resit candidates aren't relearning their pathway from scratch — they're closing specific gaps identified in their referral report.

How to use this module differently on a resit

  • Go back to your actual referral report before you start, and map its specific feedback points against the sections in this module — if your referral cited a gap in, for example, conflict avoidance or business planning, prioritise that section rather than working through everything in the original order
  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Commercial Real Estate-specific material here

Referral rates on Commercial Real Estate and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m11b.title: Valuation Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Pathway-specific preparation for Valuation candidates — professional practice, technical tools, and specialist knowledge for the APC final assessment.

sections.h: 11B.0 Understanding Your Technical Pathway Module
sections.body:
Before you work through the rest of Module 11B, it's worth understanding what this module actually is and why it sits where it does in your journey to Chartered status.

Modules 1 through 11 built your grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies — the ethics, client care, communication, health and safety, and business skills every RICS candidate needs, regardless of pathway. That knowledge is necessary, but it isn't sufficient on its own. Assessors don't just want to know that you understand client care in the abstract — they want to see you apply it specifically to the kind of work Valuation candidates actually do.

That's what this module is for. Everything from here through the end of Module 11B has been built and verified specifically against the current official RICS Valuation pathway guide — not a generic template with your pathway's name inserted. The competency structure, the legal and technical detail, and the Module 12 scenario at the end are all grounded in what Valuation candidates are genuinely tested on.

How to use this module well

  • Treat the competency structure section (11B.2) as your reference point when finalising your own declaration with your counsellor — it's a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it
  • Read every section with your own PDR experience in mind — the goal is connecting this material to what you've actually done, not memorising it in the abstract
  • Use Michael, your AI tutor, to pressure-test your answers on the scenarios that feel less familiar, not just the ones you're already confident on
  • Treat the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine practice interview question, not a reading exercise — actually formulate your answer before checking the model response

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain, in your own words, why Valuation candidates are tested the way they are — not just recite what the test covers.

sections.h: 11B.1 Introduction and Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
Welcome to Module 11B — your final period of structured learning before Module 12's revision and mock APC simulation. This module exists because technical competence in Valuation is only half of what RICS assesses at final assessment. The other half is professional practice: how you conduct yourself, manage risk, communicate with clients, run a viable business, and operate ethically and sustainably within the profession.

Valuers carry a distinct professional exposure that other pathways don't face in quite the same way — a written valuation opinion is relied on by lenders, purchasers, and courts, often for decisions involving significant sums of money, and it can be scrutinised long after the fact if a transaction goes wrong. Assessors expect Valuation candidates to demonstrate not just technical competence in arriving at a figure, but the judgement, record-keeping discipline, and professional rigour that protects both the client and the valuer if that figure is ever challenged.

Learning Outcomes

  • Explain the structure of the Valuation pathway and justify your competency selections
  • Apply health and safety principles specific to valuation inspections
  • Demonstrate working knowledge of accounting principles as they apply to Valuation practice
  • Identify and use the data sources and professional tools relied on by valuers
  • Apply RICS client care standards to valuation client relationships
  • Explain how a valuation practice plans and sustains a viable business
  • Apply conflict avoidance and dispute resolution principles to valuation-related scenarios
  • Discuss sustainability considerations specific to valuation practice
  • Practise applying this knowledge to realistic APC scenarios with Michael, your AI tutor
  • Demonstrate readiness through a full module assessment

This module assumes you have already worked through Modules 1–10 and hold a solid grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies. What follows sharpens that knowledge specifically for Valuation practice.

sections.h: 11B.2 The Valuation Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
The Valuation pathway is built around producing valuation opinions that clients, lenders, and courts can rely on — across residential, commercial, and specialist asset classes, for purposes ranging from secured lending to taxation, litigation, and financial reporting.

Mandatory competencies

Common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway: Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

Core Valuation competencies

All three required:

  • Inspection (Level 3)
  • Valuation (Level 3)
  • Measurement (Level 2)

Optional competencies

You select three to Level 3, or two to Level 3 and two to Level 2. One of your picks must come from the group of Accounting principles and procedures, Conflict avoidance, Data management, or Sustainability — you elevate one of these to a higher pathway-specific level rather than declaring all four. Beyond that, the optional list is broad: Landlord and tenant, Leasing and letting, Investment management, Development appraisals, Property management, Property finance and funding, Strategic real estate consultancy, Legal/regulatory compliance, Planning and development management, Purchase and sale, Building pathology, Capital taxation, Compulsory purchase and compensation, Construction technology and environmental services, Contaminated land, Corporate recovery and insolvency, Indirect investment vehicles, Insurance, Loan security valuation, Local taxation/assessment, Auctioneering, and Valuation of businesses and intangible assets.

Your actual selection should be driven entirely by what you do in your own role, agreed with your counsellor — not by which competencies sound most impressive.

Source: RICS Valuation Pathway Guide (published 1 December 2025) — always check your specific declaration against the current guide on the RICS website before finalising it with your counsellor, since RICS updates these periodically.

Assessors mark candidates against the level of competency claimed (Level 1: knowledge and understanding; Level 2: application of knowledge; Level 3: reasoned advice). For Valuation candidates, Level 3 means being able to defend a valuation figure — its methodology, evidence, and assumptions — with the same rigour you'd need if that figure were challenged months or years later, not simply describing how a valuation is carried out.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
Valuation inspections carry the same physical risks as any property inspection — but valuers often work alone, visiting unfamiliar properties on a tight schedule, which raises the stakes on getting basic health and safety discipline right.

Key legal framework

  • Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 — the foundation duty of care for employers and the self-employed
  • Control of Asbestos Regulations — relevant to any pre-2000 building, particularly in roof spaces and older service areas
  • Electricity at Work Regulations — relevant where a valuer needs to assess or comment on visible electrical installations
  • Occupiers' Liability Act — relevant to risks encountered on a client's or third party's premises during inspection

Practical application for valuers

Before any inspection, a competent valuer should assess the specific risks of the property type and location — a rural property with poor mobile signal and no immediate help nearby carries different risks to a city-centre office inspection. Lone working is close to universal in valuation practice, so a properly briefed lone-working policy — check-in protocols, shared location and timing information, and a clear escalation route if contact is lost — is essential professional discipline, not an optional add-on.

Valuers should also be alert to property-specific hazards uncovered during inspection itself — unstable flooring, exposed wiring, or signs of structural movement — and know when to stop an inspection rather than push through a hazard to complete it.

At Level 3, you should be able to explain how you would identify, assess, and mitigate a specific health and safety risk you've encountered in your own valuation work — not recite the regulations in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
Every RICS member needs a working grasp of accounting principles, and valuation work brings that knowledge into direct, evidence-relevant focus.

Core areas relevant to Valuation candidates

  • Reading company accounts — assessing a business's financial position where valuation evidence depends on trading performance (e.g. valuing a trading asset such as a pub, hotel, or care home using the profits method)
  • Fee structures and client money — RICS Client Money Protection requirements where fees or deposits are handled, and understanding fee bases (fixed fee vs. percentage of value) and the conflicts of interest that percentage-based fees can raise
  • VAT treatment — the option to tax and its relevance to valuations involving commercial property transactions
  • Understanding lender covenants — for secured lending valuations, understanding loan-to-value ratios and why the lender's risk appetite shapes the instruction

Practical application

A valuer using the profits method to value a trading business needs to be able to read and interpret the underlying accounts — turnover trends, adjusted net profit, and any one-off items that shouldn't be capitalised into the valuation. Being able to explain why you adjusted (or didn't adjust) a particular figure in the accounts is a common line of questioning at interview.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
Valuation is an evidence-based discipline. Assessors expect candidates to know not just that data exists, but which source is fit for which purpose, and how to weigh conflicting evidence.

Core data sources

  • HM Land Registry — title, ownership, and sold price data
  • VOA (Valuation Office Agency) — rating list and council tax band data
  • CoStar / EGi (Estates Gazette Interactive) — commercial market transactions and comparable evidence
  • RICS Comparable Evidence in Real Estate Valuation guidance note — the hierarchy of evidence, distinguishing directly comparable transactions from less direct sources
  • RICS Valuation – Global Standards (Red Book) — the mandatory framework governing methodology, reporting, and minimum content
  • Local authority planning portals — planning history and permitted development rights relevant to a subject property

Practical application

When arriving at a valuation figure, you should be able to explain your position in the hierarchy of evidence — a directly comparable, recent, arm's-length transaction of a near-identical property carries far more weight than an asking price or a dated transaction in a different location. Assessors want to see that you understand this hierarchy and can defend why you weighted your evidence the way you did, not just that you gathered comparables.

At Level 3, you're expected to reach a reasoned, defensible position when the available evidence is imperfect or conflicting — which, in practice, it usually is.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
RICS client care standards apply to every pathway, but valuation work often puts you in the position of delivering a figure the client doesn't want to hear — a lower-than-expected mortgage valuation, a disappointing probate figure, a business valuation below what a shareholder hoped for.

Core requirements

  • Clear terms of engagement agreed and confirmed in writing before work begins, including the purpose and intended user(s) of the valuation
  • A complaints handling procedure that meets RICS requirements, and that you can explain to a client if asked
  • Transparency about your independence and objectivity — checking for conflicts of interest before accepting an instruction, and being able to explain how you managed any potential conflict
  • Managing expectations proactively rather than reactively, particularly where the figure is likely to disappoint

Practical application

A common Valuation scenario at interview: a client is unhappy that your valuation came in below the figure they expected, and asks you to reconsider. Good client care here means explaining your methodology and evidence clearly and professionally, without being pressured into adjusting a figure that isn't supported by the evidence. Assessors want to see that you can hold a defensible professional line under client pressure, not that you can avoid the conversation.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
Whether you work for a large firm, a boutique valuation practice, or in-house, RICS expects every candidate to understand how their team or business sustains itself commercially.

Core areas

  • Fee income models specific to valuation — fixed fees for most instructions (percentage-based fees are generally discouraged or restricted for certain valuation types due to conflict of interest concerns)
  • Resourcing and capacity planning — valuation instructions often carry tight statutory or lender deadlines, so capacity planning matters more than in some other pathways
  • Professional indemnity insurance — understanding why PII cover, and its limits, is central to a viable valuation practice given the potential exposure of a challenged valuation
  • Quality control processes — internal review or sign-off procedures before a valuation report is issued, and why these exist

Practical application

Be ready to discuss, from your own experience, how your firm resources valuation instructions against tight deadlines, and what internal review or sign-off process exists before a report goes out to a client. Assessors are testing commercial and risk awareness — do you understand why these processes exist, not just that they exist.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
Valuation work carries a distinctive conflict risk: independence and objectivity are core to the value of a valuation opinion, and any compromise to that independence — real or perceived — undermines the whole exercise.

Core framework

  • RICS Conflict Avoidance, Management and Dispute Resolution Professional Statement
  • Independence and objectivity checks — confirming no conflict of interest before accepting every valuation instruction, with a clear record of that check
  • Common conflict scenarios — prior involvement with the property (e.g. having valued it before, or acting for the other party in a related transaction), or a fee structure that creates an incentive to reach a particular figure
  • Escalation where a conflict can't be adequately managed — the instruction should be declined, not accepted with an internal information barrier that doesn't genuinely resolve the issue

Practical application

A frequent scenario: you're asked to value a property you previously valued for a different purpose eighteen months ago, or a property where your firm also acts for the prospective purchaser. Assessors want you to identify the conflict, explain the disclosure or management steps required under RICS guidance, and recognise when a conflict is severe enough that the only proper course is to decline the instruction — not just say we would manage it carefully.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Valuation Practice
sections.body:
Sustainability has moved from a peripheral consideration to a mainstream valuation input — directly affecting comparable evidence, investment demand, and increasingly the valuation figure itself.

Key areas

  • EPC ratings — their growing role in comparable evidence and investment decision-making, particularly the green premium and brown discount effects observed in some sectors
  • MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards) — the regulatory backdrop affecting lettability, and therefore value, of poorly-rated commercial assets
  • Sustainability and ESG in valuation reporting — RICS professional standards increasingly expect valuers to consider and comment on sustainability factors as part of a valuation, where relevant to the asset and market
  • Physical climate risk — increasingly a comparable-evidence and risk consideration for certain locations and asset types (e.g. flood risk)

Practical application

Be ready to discuss how you would reflect a poor EPC rating or identified sustainability risk in a valuation figure — whether through an adjustment to comparable evidence, a stated assumption, or a qualification in your report — rather than either ignoring it or claiming a precise, unsupportable discount. Assessors are testing whether you treat sustainability as a genuine valuation input, not a box-ticking add-on.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
This section is your space to practise applying everything above to realistic APC-style scenarios, working through them with Michael, your AI tutor.

Michael can run you through scenario-based questions specific to Valuation — a challenged mortgage valuation, a conflict of interest scenario, a disputed comparable evidence position, a sustainability-driven valuation judgement — and probe your answers the way an assessor would: asking you to justify your reasoning, challenging your position, and pushing you past description into advice.

How to use this section effectively

  • Bring real examples from your own PDR wherever possible — Michael will help you structure and sharpen them, but the substance should be yours
  • Practise the follow-up that asks what you would advise, not just what happened — assessors mark judgement, not narrative
  • Use Michael to stress-test weak points — if you're less confident on conflict scenarios or defending a figure under pressure, spend deliberate time there rather than defaulting to your strongest area

Open a session with Michael now and work through at least three Valuation-specific scenarios before moving to the module assessment.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
Complete the following ten questions to check your readiness for Module 12. These mirror the style and difficulty of real APC interview questions on the Valuation pathway — read each one as if a panel member had just asked it, and answer as you would in the room.

  1. A client is unhappy that your valuation came in below their expectations and asks you to reconsider the figure. How would you handle this, consistent with RICS client care and independence requirements?
  2. You're asked to value a property you valued for a different client eighteen months ago. Talk me through how you'd identify and manage this potential conflict.
  3. Explain the hierarchy of comparable evidence, and how you would defend your position if the other side in a dispute relied on a different set of comparables.
  4. A commercial property you're valuing has a poor EPC rating. How would you reflect this in your valuation, and what would you disclose in your report?
  5. Outline the health and safety considerations you would apply before conducting a lone inspection of an unfamiliar rural property.
  6. You're using the profits method to value a trading business, and the accounts show a one-off exceptional item. How would you treat this in your valuation?
  7. Explain the minimum reporting requirements you would expect a compliant valuation report to meet, and what would make a valuation non-compliant.
  8. A lender challenges your secured lending valuation six months after a loan default, alleging professional negligence. Talk me through how you would respond.
  9. Describe the internal quality control or sign-off process your firm applies before a valuation report is issued, and why this matters.
  10. Explain why percentage-based fees are generally discouraged for certain types of valuation instruction, and what conflict of interest this addresses.

Once you've worked through all ten and are satisfied with your answers — ideally after testing them against Michael's follow-up questions — you are ready for Module 12 — Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Valuation-specific material here

Referral rates on Valuation and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m11b.title: Infrastructure Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Infrastructure practice combines engineering-scale technical complexity with the full weight of RICS professional obligations — client care, commercial judgement, sustainability, and dispute management across multi-year, multi-party schemes. This module sharpens every mandatory competency through the specific lens of Infrastructure work, completing your preparation for Module 12.
