sections.h: 11B.2 The Management Consultancy Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
Management Consultancy is for those trained in economics, business, and management skills who provide consultancy advice to identify and implement business solutions to real estate problems, at any stage of the land and property lifecycle.

Mandatory competencies (common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway):
Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

Core competencies (all four required): Business case; Business planning; Consultancy services; Research methodologies and techniques.

Optional competencies: you select three, from a broad list including Business alignment, Change management, Corporate finance, Corporate recovery and insolvency, Data management, Development appraisals, Development/project briefs, Economic development, Managing resources, Performance management, Programming and planning, Property finance and funding, Smart cities and intelligent buildings, Strategic real estate consultancy, and Workspace strategy. Plus one further competency to Level 2 from either the core or optional list.

A note worth remembering: RICS specifically advises against choosing both Strategic real estate consultancy and a closely overlapping competency together, given their significant overlap — your selection should reflect genuinely distinct areas of your actual experience.

Your actual selection should be driven entirely by what you do in your own role, agreed with your counsellor — not by which competencies sound most impressive. Note that there is no separate Associate (AssocRICS) pathway for Management Consultancy — candidates interested in a similar area at Associate level are directed toward Project Management instead.

Source: RICS Management Consultancy Pathway Guide (published December 2025) — always check your specific declaration against the current guide on the RICS website before finalising it with your counsellor, since RICS updates these periodically.

Assessors mark candidates against the level of competency claimed (Level 1: knowledge and understanding; Level 2: application of knowledge; Level 3: reasoned advice, depth and synthesis). For Management Consultancy candidates, Level 3 means being able to defend a strategic recommendation with the analytical rigour and independence expected of a senior colleague — not simply describing a consultancy process in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
Management Consultancy work is often desk- and analysis-based, but candidates should still be able to demonstrate genuine health and safety understanding, particularly where consultancy work involves site visits or client premises inspections as part of a wider engagement.

Key legal framework:
  • Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 — the foundation duty of care for employers and the self-employed
  • Occupiers' Liability Act — relevant to any client site visits undertaken as part of a consultancy engagement
Practical application for Management Consultancy candidates:
Even where the bulk of your work is analytical or advisory, you should be able to explain how you assess and manage health and safety risk whenever a site visit or client premises inspection forms part of an engagement — treating this with the same discipline as a purely technical pathway would, rather than assuming it's less relevant because your primary focus is strategic advice.

At Level 3, you should be able to explain how you would identify, assess, and mitigate a specific health and safety risk relevant to your own consultancy work — not recite the regulations in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
Every RICS member needs a working grasp of accounting principles, and Management Consultancy practice brings that knowledge into direct focus, given the discipline's core reliance on business case development.

Core areas relevant to Management Consultancy candidates:
  • Business case financial analysis — the financial standards and metrics needed to build a credible, defensible business case for a client
  • Reading company accounts — assessing a client organisation's financial position where relevant to strategic recommendations
  • Cost-benefit analysis — a core analytical tool for consultancy recommendations, and understanding its limitations
  • Return on investment and payback analysis — common financial measures used to justify a recommended course of action
Practical application:
A Management Consultancy professional building a business case needs to present a financial analysis that would genuinely withstand scrutiny from a client's own finance function — not just property-specific reasoning, but the financial rigour and standards that a board or senior stakeholder would expect before committing significant investment.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
Management Consultancy practice draws on a distinctive set of data sources spanning research, market intelligence, and organisational performance.

Core data sources:
  • Primary research — surveys, interviews, and stakeholder consultation conducted specifically for a consultancy engagement
  • Secondary research and market intelligence — published reports, industry benchmarking, and economic data used to support strategic recommendations
  • Client organisational data — internal performance, cost, and operational data relevant to the specific engagement
  • Academic and professional research methodology standards — underpinning the credibility of any research-based recommendation
Practical application:
When presenting a strategic recommendation, a Management Consultancy professional should be able to explain exactly which research methodology was used — the sample size, data sources, and any limitations — and be transparent about how confident the underlying evidence genuinely is, rather than presenting a recommendation with more certainty than the evidence actually supports.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
RICS client care standards apply to every pathway, but Management Consultancy work often means presenting recommendations that a client's senior stakeholders may not want to hear, requiring particular skill in maintaining the relationship while holding a professionally independent position.

Core requirements:
  • Clear terms of engagement, agreed and confirmed in writing before work begins, including the scope and methodology of any research to be undertaken
  • A complaints handling procedure that meets RICS requirements, and that you can explain to a client if asked
  • Transparent fee structures appropriate to the nature and duration of the consultancy engagement
  • Managing expectations proactively, particularly where research findings or strategic analysis produce a conclusion the client didn't expect or want
Practical application:
A common Management Consultancy scenario at interview: a client challenges the methodology behind a research-based recommendation because they're uncomfortable with the conclusion. Good client care here means engaging with the challenge professionally and transparently, defending the methodology on its merits, and being honest about genuine limitations — rather than either becoming defensive or quietly softening the recommendation to keep the client comfortable.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
Whether you work for a large multidisciplinary firm or a specialist management consultancy, RICS expects every candidate to understand how their business sustains itself commercially.

Core areas:
  • Fee structures specific to consultancy work — time-based, fixed-fee, or value-based fee models, each carrying different commercial and independence considerations
  • Resourcing and capacity planning — consultancy engagements often require specialist research or analytical resource alongside core project delivery
  • Business development — how consultancy practices win and retain instructions in a relationship- and reputation-driven market
  • Risk management at the business level — professional indemnity insurance considerations given the strategic, high-stakes nature of consultancy advice
Practical application:
Be ready to discuss, from your own experience, how your practice structures its fees for consultancy engagements, and how it manages the tension between value-based fees and maintaining genuine independence in the advice given. Assessors are testing commercial and ethical awareness together.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
Management Consultancy work carries a distinctive independence risk: the value of strategic advice depends entirely on it being genuinely objective, and any compromise to that independence — real or perceived — undermines the whole engagement.

Core framework:
  • RICS Conflict Avoidance, Management and Dispute Resolution Professional Statement
  • Common conflict scenarios — advising multiple parties with competing interests on related matters, or a fee structure that could incentivise a particular recommendation
  • The dispute resolution ladder: negotiation → mediation → independent expert determination or arbitration → litigation as a last resort
  • Managing genuine challenge to a recommendation professionally — distinguishing legitimate scrutiny of methodology from pressure to change a conclusion for reasons unrelated to the evidence
Practical application:
A frequent scenario: a client challenges your research methodology because they're unhappy with where your recommendation leads. Assessors want you to explain how you would engage with that challenge on its actual merits — defending genuinely sound methodology, acknowledging genuine limitations honestly — rather than either capitulating to pressure or dismissing legitimate scrutiny defensively.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Management Consultancy Practice
sections.body:
Sustainability increasingly forms a core strand of the strategic advice Management Consultancy professionals are asked to provide.

Key areas:
  • Sustainability as a strategic business driver — increasingly a core input to strategic real estate decisions, not a separate add-on consideration
  • ESG-informed recommendations — client organisations increasingly expect consultancy advice to be explicitly informed by ESG commitments and reporting requirements
  • Economic and social development considerations — relevant where consultancy advice touches on regeneration, economic development, or community impact
  • Balancing sustainability ambition against commercial reality — a genuine trade-off that strategic advice needs to navigate, not resolve by ignoring one side
Practical application:
Be ready to discuss how you would build a strategic recommendation that genuinely integrates sustainability considerations with commercial and operational priorities — explaining the trade-offs honestly, rather than treating sustainability as either automatically decisive or as an afterthought layered on top of a decision already made.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
This section is your space to practise applying everything above to realistic APC-style scenarios, working through them with Michael, your AI tutor.

Michael can run you through scenario-based questions specific to Management Consultancy — a challenged research methodology, an independence-under-pressure scenario, a business case defence, a sustainability-versus-commercial trade-off — and probe your answers the way an assessor would: asking you to justify your reasoning, challenging your position, and pushing you past description into advice.

How to use this section effectively:
  • Bring real examples from your own PDR wherever possible — Michael will help you structure and sharpen them, but the substance should be yours
  • Practise the "what would you advise" follow-up, not just "what happened" — assessors mark judgement, not narrative
  • Use Michael to stress-test weak points — if you're less confident on research methodology or independence scenarios, spend deliberate time there rather than defaulting to your strongest area
Open a session with Michael now and work through at least three Management Consultancy-specific scenarios before moving to the module assessment.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
Complete the following ten questions to check your readiness for Module 12. These mirror the style and difficulty of real APC interview questions on the Management Consultancy pathway — read each one as if a panel member had just asked it, and answer as you would in the room.

  1. A board member challenges the research methodology underpinning your strategic recommendation. How would you respond?
  2. Explain how you would build a business case that would genuinely withstand scrutiny from a client's own finance function.
  3. A client is unhappy with where your research-based recommendation leads and pressures you to reconsider. How would you maintain your independence?
  4. Describe the difference between primary and secondary research, and how you would combine them in a consultancy engagement.
  5. Outline the health and safety considerations relevant to a client site visit undertaken as part of a consultancy engagement.
  6. Explain how you would integrate sustainability considerations into a strategic recommendation without treating them as either decisive or an afterthought.
  7. How would a value-based fee structure on a consultancy engagement create a potential conflict of interest, and how would you manage it?
  8. Describe how you would present cost-benefit analysis to a client, including its limitations.
  9. Explain why RICS advises against selecting both Strategic real estate consultancy and a closely overlapping competency together, and how you'd justify your own selection.
  10. A client organisation's internal data conflicts with your external research findings. How would you reconcile this in your final recommendation?
Once you've worked through all ten and are satisfied with your answers — ideally after testing them against Michael's follow-up questions — you're ready for Module 12: Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

sections.h: 11B.12 If You've Been Referred: What This Module Means for You
sections.body:
If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Management Consultancy professional. It's specific, actionable feedback about what didn't land clearly enough in a particular interview, on a particular day, in front of a particular panel. Most successful resit candidates aren't relearning their pathway from scratch — they're closing specific gaps identified in their referral report.

How to use this module differently on a resit

  • Go back to your actual referral report before you start, and map its specific feedback points against the sections in this module — if your referral cited a gap in, for example, conflict avoidance or business planning, prioritise that section rather than working through everything in the original order
  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Management Consultancy-specific material here

Referral rates on Management Consultancy and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m11b.title: Land and Resources Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Land and Resources is one of the broadest RICS pathways — combining environmental, geospatial, minerals and waste, planning and development, and rural expertise. This module sharpens every mandatory competency through the specific lens of your Land and Resources specialism, completing your preparation for Module 12.

sections.h: 11B.0 Understanding Your Technical Pathway Module
sections.body:
Before you work through the rest of Module 11B, it's worth understanding what this module actually is and why it sits where it does in your journey to Chartered status.

Modules 1 through 11 built your grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies — the ethics, client care, communication, health and safety, and business skills every RICS candidate needs, regardless of pathway. That knowledge is necessary, but it isn't sufficient on its own. Assessors don't just want to know that you understand client care in the abstract — they want to see you apply it specifically to the kind of work Land and Resources candidates actually do.

That's what this module is for. Everything from here through the end of Module 11B has been built and verified specifically against the current official RICS Land and Resources pathway guide — not a generic template with your pathway's name inserted. The competency structure, the legal and technical detail, and the Module 12 scenario at the end are all grounded in what Land and Resources candidates are genuinely tested on.

How to use this module well

  • Treat the competency structure section (11B.2) as your reference point when finalising your own declaration with your counsellor — it's a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it
  • Read every section with your own PDR experience in mind — the goal is connecting this material to what you've actually done, not memorising it in the abstract
  • Use Michael, your AI tutor, to pressure-test your answers on the scenarios that feel less familiar, not just the ones you're already confident on
  • Treat the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine practice interview question, not a reading exercise — actually formulate your answer before checking the model response

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain, in your own words, why Land and Resources candidates are tested the way they are — not just recite what the test covers.

sections.h: 11B.1 Introduction and Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
Welcome to Module 11B — your final period of structured learning before Module 12's revision and mock APC simulation. This module exists because technical competence in Land and Resources is only half of what RICS assesses at final assessment. The other half is professional practice: how you conduct yourself, manage risk, communicate with clients, run a viable business, and operate ethically and sustainably within the profession.

Land and Resources is one of the broadest RICS pathways, combining environmental, geospatial, minerals and waste management, planning and development, and rural expertise into a single "land professional" chartered surveyor. Assessors expect candidates on this pathway to demonstrate not just deep technical competence in their chosen specialism, but the breadth of professional judgement, procedural precision, and stakeholder management skill that comes with advising across the entire land and property lifecycle — from registration and mapping through to development, remediation, and re-use.

By the end of this module, you will be able to:
  • Explain the structure of the Land and Resources pathway and justify your competency selections
  • Apply health and safety principles specific to land and resources practice
  • Demonstrate working knowledge of accounting principles as they apply to this pathway
  • Identify and use the data sources and professional tools relied on by land and resources practitioners
  • Apply RICS client care standards to land and resources client relationships
  • Explain how a land and resources practice plans and sustains a viable business
  • Apply conflict avoidance and dispute resolution principles to relevant scenarios
  • Discuss sustainability considerations specific to land and resources
  • Practise applying this knowledge to realistic APC scenarios with Michael, your AI tutor
  • Demonstrate readiness through a full module assessment
This module assumes you have already worked through Modules 1–10 and hold a solid grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies. What follows sharpens that knowledge specifically for Land and Resources practice.

sections.h: 11B.2 The Land and Resources Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
The Land and Resources pathway is designed to be applicable across a wide-ranging group of land and resource-related sectors, combining the best of the environmental, geospatial surveying, minerals and waste management, planning and development, and rural professional groups.

Mandatory competencies (common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway):
Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

Unlike many other pathways, Land and Resources doesn't split into separate "core" and "optional" categories — instead, you select five competencies to Level 3 and one to Level 2 from a single broad technical list: Access and rights over land, Agriculture, Big data, Cadastre and land administration, Client care (must be taken to Level 3 if chosen here), Compulsory purchase and compensation, Consultancy services, Contaminated land, Development appraisals, Economic development, Energy and renewable resources, Engineering surveying, Environmental management, Geodesy, GIS, Hydrographic surveying, Inspection, Land use and diversification, Landlord and tenant, Legal/regulatory compliance, Management of the natural environment and landscape, Masterplanning and urban design, Measurement, Minerals management, Planning and development management, Property management, Risk management, Smart cities and intelligent buildings, Spatial planning policy and infrastructure, Strategic real estate consultancy, Surveying and mapping, Sustainability, Valuation, and Waste management.

Plus two further competencies to Level 2 from the full list of technical competencies, including any not already chosen.

RICS identifies 12 competencies as the primary skillset for a "land professional" worth considering first: access and rights over land, cadastre and land administration, compulsory purchase and compensation, GIS, inspection, landlord and tenant, legal/regulatory compliance, planning and development management, property management, surveying and mapping, sustainability, and valuation.

Chartered alternative designations are available for candidates taking specific competencies to Level 3: Engineering surveying → Chartered Engineering Surveyor; Environmental management → Chartered Environmental Surveyor; Hydrographic surveying → Chartered Hydrographic Surveyor; Minerals management or Waste management → Chartered Minerals Surveyor; Planning and development management or Spatial planning policy and infrastructure → Chartered Planning and Development Surveyor; Surveying and mapping → Chartered Land Surveyor. Candidates not pursuing one of these designations receive the standard "Chartered Surveyor" title.

Your actual selection should be driven entirely by what you do in your own role, agreed with your counsellor — not by which competencies sound most impressive. Given the sheer breadth of this pathway, resist the temptation to select competencies too widely spread across unrelated specialisms — a coherent, defensible selection tied to your genuine experience is far stronger than a scattered one.

Source: RICS Land and Resources Pathway Guide (published December 2025, Version 1.4) — always check your specific declaration against the current guide on the RICS website before finalising it with your counsellor, since RICS updates these periodically.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
Given the breadth of this pathway, health and safety risk varies enormously depending on specialism — from office-based GIS and cadastral work to fieldwork on active mineral extraction sites, contaminated land, or remote rural locations.

Key legal framework:
  • Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 — the foundation duty of care for employers and the self-employed
  • Site-specific regulation depending on specialism — including regulation relevant to contaminated land investigation, minerals and waste site safety, and construction/development site hazards
  • Lone-working considerations — particularly relevant to rural, environmental, and remote site inspection work
Practical application for Land and Resources candidates:
A competent practitioner assesses the specific risks of their own specialism and site — contaminated land investigation carries very different risks to a rural boundary survey or an office-based planning appraisal. Whatever your specific area of practice, you should be able to explain how you identify, assess, and mitigate the specific health and safety risks relevant to your own work, rather than defaulting to generic property-inspection risk language that doesn't actually reflect what you do.

At Level 3, you should be able to give a specific, real example from your own experience — not recite the regulations in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
Every RICS member needs a working grasp of accounting principles, and Land and Resources practice brings that knowledge into focus around development viability, minerals/waste economics, and land-related financial appraisal.

Core areas relevant to Land and Resources candidates:
  • Development and viability appraisal financial principles — relevant to planning and development-focused practice
  • Minerals and waste economics — royalties, rents, and rating issues relevant to extraction or waste management specialisms
  • Grant and funding mechanisms — relevant to environmental, economic development, and regeneration-focused work
  • Compensation valuation principles — relevant to compulsory purchase and access/rights work
Practical application:
Whatever your specific specialism, you should be able to explain the financial principles most relevant to your own area of practice — for example, a minerals specialist explaining royalty and rating structures, or a planning-focused practitioner explaining viability appraisal inputs — rather than giving a generic answer disconnected from your actual work.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
Land and Resources practice draws on an unusually broad range of data sources, reflecting the pathway's combination of specialisms.

Core data sources:
  • HM Land Registry and cadastral records — title, ownership, and boundary information
  • GIS and mapping platforms — used across nearly every specialism within this pathway
  • Environmental and contamination databases — relevant to environmental management and contaminated land work
  • Planning policy documents and precedent decisions — relevant to planning and development-focused practice
  • Sector-specific technical data — mineral resource data, waste management regulatory data, or agricultural/rural market data depending on specialism
Practical application:
Whatever your specific specialism, you should be able to explain exactly which data sources you rely on, why they're fit for purpose, and their limitations — a genuine, specific answer grounded in your own practice, rather than a generic list spanning specialisms you don't actually work in.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
RICS client care standards apply to every pathway, but Land and Resources work often involves a genuinely varied client base — private landowners, developers, local authorities, utility companies, and government bodies — sometimes with directly competing interests.

Core requirements:
  • Clear terms of engagement agreed and confirmed in writing before work begins
  • A complaints handling procedure that meets RICS requirements, and that you can explain to a client if asked
  • Transparent fee structures appropriate to the nature of the instruction
  • Managing expectations proactively, particularly where technical findings (environmental, planning, or legal) are likely to disappoint the client
Practical application:
A common scenario at interview: a client is unhappy that a technical finding — a contamination result, a rights of light constraint, a planning policy conclusion — limits what they hoped to achieve. Good client care here means explaining the finding clearly and professionally, without softening a position that isn't supported by the evidence, while helping the client understand their realistic options going forward.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
Whether you work for a specialist land consultancy, a multidisciplinary firm, a local authority, or in-house for a landowner or developer, RICS expects every candidate to understand how their business sustains itself commercially.

Core areas:
  • Fee structures specific to your specialism — fixed fees, time-based fees, or value-based fees, each with different commercial and independence considerations
  • Resourcing and capacity planning — particularly relevant given how project-based and often unpredictable land and resources work can be
  • Business development — how practices in this space win and retain instructions in a specialist, relationship-driven market
  • Risk management at the business level — professional indemnity insurance considerations relevant to your specific specialism
Practical application:
Be ready to discuss, from your own experience, how your practice or team resources instructions in your specialism, and how fee structures are set and disclosed to avoid conflicts of interest. Assessors are testing commercial awareness specific to your actual area of practice.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
Given this pathway's breadth, dispute patterns vary by specialism — but boundary and access disputes, planning disagreements, contamination liability disputes, and rights-related conflicts are all common across the pathway generally.

Core framework:
  • RICS Conflict Avoidance, Management and Dispute Resolution Professional Statement
  • Common dispute scenarios across specialisms — boundary and access disputes, rights of light claims, contamination liability disagreements, and planning or compulsory purchase disputes
  • The dispute resolution ladder: negotiation → mediation → expert determination, arbitration, or a public inquiry (depending on specialism) → litigation as a last resort
  • Understanding that some disputes in this pathway (particularly rights-related claims) carry genuine legal risk that planning permission or good intentions don't eliminate
Practical application:
A frequent scenario across several specialisms in this pathway: a development risks infringing a neighbouring right — whether access, light, or another easement-based interest — and the client needs advice on how to manage that risk before it becomes a formal dispute. Assessors want you to explain the specific legal framework relevant to the right in question, the realistic remedies available to the affected party, and how early, professional engagement reduces risk — not just that "disputes should be avoided" in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Land and Resources Practice
sections.body:
Sustainability runs through nearly every specialism within this pathway, from environmental management and minerals/waste through to rural land use and planning.

Key areas:
  • Sustainability within your specific specialism — the specific sustainability drivers, regulation, and practice relevant to your area (e.g. biodiversity net gain in environmental/rural contexts, embodied carbon in planning and development, restoration standards in minerals and waste)
  • Whole-life and lifecycle considerations — relevant across most specialisms in this pathway
  • Regulatory and policy drivers — national and international legislation, regulation, and taxation affecting sustainability in your area of practice
  • Balancing sustainability against commercial and practical realities — a genuine trade-off relevant across the pathway's different specialisms
Practical application:
Be ready to discuss a specific sustainability consideration genuinely relevant to your own specialism — not a generic sustainability answer disconnected from your actual practice area. Assessors are testing depth in your actual specialism, not breadth across the whole pathway.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
This section is your space to practise applying everything above to realistic APC-style scenarios, working through them with Michael, your AI tutor.

Michael can run you through scenario-based questions specific to Land and Resources — tailored to your specific specialism within the pathway, whether environmental, geospatial, minerals and waste, planning, or rural-adjacent — and probe your answers the way an assessor would: asking you to justify your reasoning, challenging your position, and pushing you past description into advice.

How to use this section effectively:
  • Bring real examples from your own PDR wherever possible, specific to your actual specialism — Michael will help you structure and sharpen them, but the substance should be yours
  • Practise the "what would you advise" follow-up, not just "what happened" — assessors mark judgement, not narrative
  • Use Michael to stress-test weak points specific to your specialism, rather than trying to cover the entire breadth of this pathway generically
Open a session with Michael now and work through at least three scenarios specific to your own Land and Resources specialism before moving to the module assessment.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
Complete the following ten questions to check your readiness for Module 12. These mirror the style and difficulty of real APC interview questions on the Land and Resources pathway — read each one as if a panel member had just asked it, and answer as you would in the room.

  1. A client is unhappy that a technical finding (environmental, planning, or legal) limits what they hoped to achieve. How would you handle this conversation professionally?
  2. Explain the health and safety considerations specific to your own specialism within this pathway, with a real example.
  3. Describe a boundary, access, or rights-related dispute you've encountered, and how you approached resolving it.
  4. Explain a sustainability consideration genuinely relevant to your specific specialism, and how you would advise a client on it.
  5. How would you assess and communicate the limitations of the data sources you rely on in your own area of practice?
  6. Describe the fee structure your practice or team uses for instructions in your specialism, and any conflict of interest considerations.
  7. Explain the financial or economic principles most relevant to your specific specialism (e.g. viability appraisal, minerals royalties, compensation valuation).
  8. A development risks infringing a neighbouring right (access, light, or similar). How would you advise a client to manage this risk?
  9. Explain which chartered alternative designation, if any, is relevant to your competency selection, and why.
  10. Describe how your competency selection reflects your actual day-to-day practice, and why you avoided spreading your selection too broadly across unrelated specialisms.
Once you've worked through all ten and are satisfied with your answers — ideally after testing them against Michael's follow-up questions — you're ready for Module 12: Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Land and Resources professional. m11b.title: Building Control Pathway — Professional Practice and Technical Foundations
m11b.intro: Building Control surveyors carry a direct public safety responsibility — ensuring building regulations are followed at every stage of design and construction, and stepping in decisively when they aren't. This module sharpens every mandatory competency through the specific lens of Building Control practice, completing your preparation for Module 12.

sections.body:
Before you work through the rest of Module 11B, it's worth understanding what this module actually is and why it sits where it does in your journey to Chartered status.

Modules 1 through 11 built your grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies — the ethics, client care, communication, health and safety, and business skills every RICS candidate needs, regardless of pathway. Assessors don't just want to know that you understand client care in the abstract — they want to see you apply it specifically to the kind of work Building Control candidates actually do.

That's what this module is for. Everything from here through the end of Module 11B has been built and verified specifically against the current official RICS Building Control pathway guide — not a generic template with your pathway's name inserted. The competency structure, the legal and technical detail, and the Module 12 scenario at the end are all grounded in what Building Control candidates are genuinely tested on.

How to use this module well

  • Treat the competency structure section (11B.2) as your reference point when finalising your own declaration with your counsellor — it's a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it
  • Read every section with your own PDR experience in mind — the goal is connecting this material to what you've actually done, not memorising it in the abstract
  • Use Michael, your AI tutor, to pressure-test your answers on the scenarios that feel less familiar, not just the ones you're already confident on
  • Treat the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine practice interview question, not a reading exercise — actually formulate your answer before checking the model response

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain, in your own words, why Building Control candidates are tested the way they are — not just recite what the test covers.

sections.h: 11B.1 Introduction and Learning Outcomes
sections.body:
Welcome to Module 11B — your final period of structured learning before Module 12's revision and mock APC simulation. This module exists because technical competence in Building Control is only half of what RICS assesses at final assessment. The other half is professional practice: how you conduct yourself, manage risk, communicate with clients, run a viable business, and operate ethically and sustainably within the profession.

Building Control surveyors carry a public safety responsibility that few other pathways share so directly — ensuring building regulations and other legislation are followed at every stage of design and construction, and stepping in decisively when they aren't. Whether working in the public or private sector, you're relied on for judgement calls that genuinely protect public safety, from routine compliance checking through to advising on dangerous structures and enforcement action. Assessors expect Building Control candidates to demonstrate not just technical fluency in inspection and fire safety, but the procedural precision, currency of knowledge, and professional authority that this responsibility demands.

By the end of this module, you will be able to:
  • Explain the structure of the Building Control pathway and justify your competency selections
  • Apply health and safety principles specific to Building Control practice
  • Demonstrate working knowledge of accounting principles as they apply to this pathway
  • Identify and use the data sources and professional tools relied on by Building Control practitioners
  • Apply RICS client care standards to Building Control client and stakeholder relationships
  • Explain how a Building Control practice or team plans and sustains a viable business
  • Apply conflict avoidance and dispute resolution principles to enforcement and compliance scenarios
  • Discuss sustainability considerations specific to Building Control
  • Practise applying this knowledge to realistic APC scenarios with Michael, your AI tutor
  • Demonstrate readiness through a full module assessment
This module assumes you have already worked through Modules 1–10 and hold a solid grounding in the eleven mandatory competencies. What follows sharpens that knowledge specifically for Building Control practice.

sections.h: 11B.2 The Building Control Pathway: Structure and Competency Selection
sections.body:
Building Control surveyors ensure that building regulations and other legislation are followed in the design and construction of new and altered buildings, working alongside architects, designers, builders, and contractors from conception through to completion and use.

Mandatory competencies (common to all APC candidates regardless of pathway):
Ethics, RICS Rules of Conduct and professionalism (Level 3); Client care (Level 2); Communication and negotiation (Level 2); Health and safety (Level 2); Accounting principles and procedures (Level 1); Business planning (Level 1); Conflict avoidance, management and dispute resolution procedures (Level 1); Data management (Level 1); Diversity, inclusion and teamworking (Level 1); Inclusive environments (Level 1); Sustainability (Level 1). Source: RICS Requirements and Competencies Guide: Chartered framework (published December 2025, amended March 2026)

Core competencies (all four required, Level 3): Building control inspections; Fire safety; Inspection; Legal/regulatory compliance.

Optional competencies: two to Level 3 and one to Level 2, from: BIM management, Building pathology, Client care (to Level 3) or Data management (grouped as one choice), Conservation and restoration, Construction technology and environmental services, Contaminated land, Measurement, Planning and development management, Risk management, Sustainability, and Works progress and quality management.

Plus one further competency to Level 2 from the full list of technical competencies, including any not already chosen from the optional list.

Mandatory competency elevation: Building Control is unusual in allowing you to elevate up to two mandatory competencies to a higher level as part of your optional selection — for example, taking Client care to Level 3 or Health and safety to Level 2, where your role genuinely supports it. Most RICS pathways allow at most one mandatory competency to be elevated via the optional list; Building Control is one of the few pathways that explicitly permits two. If you use this flexibility, your submission must include evidence for each elevated level — the same standard of depth and application assessors expect for any Level 2 or Level 3 claim.

Chartered alternative designation: unlike many other pathways, this one isn't optional — all candidates qualifying through Building Control, whether working in the public or private sector, are automatically entitled to use the designation "Chartered Building Control Surveyor."

Your actual selection should be driven entirely by what you do in your own role, agreed with your counsellor — not by which competencies sound most impressive.

Source: RICS Building Control Pathway Guide (published December 2025, Version 1.2) — always check your specific declaration against the current guide on the RICS website before finalising it with your counsellor, since RICS updates these periodically.

Assessors mark candidates against the level of competency claimed (Level 1: knowledge and understanding; Level 2: application of knowledge; Level 3: reasoned advice, depth and synthesis). For Building Control candidates, Level 3 means being able to exercise the same authoritative judgement a senior colleague would when a project fails to meet standards or a genuine safety issue is found on site — not simply describing the inspection process.

sections.h: 11B.3 Health and Safety in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
Building Control surveyors work across live construction sites at every stage, and are frequently called on to inspect potentially dangerous structures — carrying a distinctive dual responsibility for their own safety and the public's.

Key legal framework:
  • Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 — the foundation duty of care for employers and the self-employed
  • Construction (Design and Management) Regulations (CDM) — relevant to coordinating safely with contractors on live sites
  • Powers relating to dangerous structures under the Building Act 1984 — a distinctive Building Control responsibility involving direct public safety risk
Practical application for Building Control candidates:
A competent practitioner treats a live construction site inspection, and especially a dangerous structure inspection, with heightened caution — structural instability, fire-damaged buildings, and demolition sites all carry acute risk that requires careful, case-specific assessment before entering. Given how frequently Building Control surveyors are the ones called to assess a structure others have already deemed unsafe, this isn't a generic property inspection risk profile.

At Level 3, you should be able to explain how you would identify, assess, and mitigate a specific health and safety risk you've encountered in your own Building Control work — not recite the regulations in the abstract.

sections.h: 11B.4 Accounting Principles in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
Every RICS member needs a working grasp of accounting principles, and Building Control practice brings that knowledge into focus around fee-setting and, where relevant, recovering enforcement costs.

Core areas relevant to Building Control candidates:
  • Fee structures for building control services — particularly relevant where competing with registered building control approvers in a mixed public/private market
  • Cost recovery in enforcement — where a local authority undertakes remedial work itself and recovers costs from a non-compliant owner
  • Basic business accounting — relevant to private sector Building Control practices operating commercially
  • Client money handling — where relevant to fee arrangements
Practical application:
Whether working in the public or private sector, a Building Control surveyor should understand how their service is priced and, on the enforcement side, how costs are recovered when a local authority steps in to carry out remedial work itself — a distinctive financial mechanism not found in most other pathways.

sections.h: 11B.5 Data Sources and Professional Tools in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
Building Control practice draws on a distinctive set of data sources centred on regulatory compliance and construction standards.

Core data sources:
  • Building Regulations and Approved Documents — the core technical standards governing compliance
  • The Building Act 1984 and Building Safety Act 2022 — the statutory framework for enforcement powers, notably reshaped by the Building Safety Act
  • Local authority and Building Safety Regulator guidance — particularly relevant given the evolving higher-risk building regime
  • RICS professional guidance — relevant to inspection, fire safety, and enforcement practice
Practical application:
Given how significantly the regulatory landscape has shifted since the Building Safety Act 2022 — extended enforcement time limits, new compliance and stop notice powers, personal liability provisions for company officers — Building Control candidates should be able to explain not just the current rules, but which recent changes reshaped them, rather than relying on training or knowledge that predates these reforms.

sections.h: 11B.6 Client Care in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
RICS client care standards apply to every pathway, but Building Control work involves a distinctive tension: the surveyor often has to give advice, and sometimes take enforcement action, that a client or building owner doesn't want to hear.

Core requirements:
  • Clear terms of engagement (in the private sector) or clear communication of statutory role and process (in the public sector), agreed and confirmed before work begins
  • A complaints handling procedure that meets RICS requirements, and that you can explain to a client if asked
  • Transparent, professional communication when non-compliant work or a dangerous structure is identified
  • Managing expectations proactively where enforcement action may be necessary
Practical application:
A common scenario at interview: an owner is unhappy that their completed work has been found non-compliant and now faces potentially costly remedial requirements. Good client care here means explaining the finding and the realistic options clearly and professionally — including the possibility of a regularisation certificate where relevant — without softening a genuine compliance issue to keep the client comfortable.

sections.h: 11B.7 Business Planning in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
Whether you work for a local authority, a private registered building control approver, or a specialist consultancy, RICS expects every candidate to understand how their business or function sustains itself commercially.

Core areas:
  • Fee structures in a competitive market — since the introduction of competition in building control, public authorities and private approvers compete for instructions, changing the commercial dynamics of the sector
  • Resourcing and capacity planning — particularly relevant given the volume and unpredictability of inspection demand
  • Business development — how a Building Control function or private practice wins and retains instructions
  • Risk management at the business level — professional indemnity and liability considerations given the public safety dimension of the role
Practical application:
Be ready to discuss, from your own experience, how your organisation prices and resources building control instructions, and how it competes (or operates, in the public sector context) within the current market structure. Assessors are testing commercial awareness specific to this pathway's distinctive market.

sections.h: 11B.8 Conflict Avoidance in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
Building Control work generates a distinctive pattern of dispute — disagreements over compliance findings, enforcement notices, and dangerous structure determinations are all common, sometimes escalating to formal appeal.

Core framework:
  • RICS Conflict Avoidance, Management and Dispute Resolution Professional Statement
  • Common dispute scenarios — disagreement over whether work complies with regulations, disputes over enforcement notices, and appeals against Section 35 or Section 36 notices
  • The formal appeal route — appeals against certain notices can be made, generally within a set time limit, to the appropriate court or tribunal
  • Understanding statutory time limits precisely — several distinct deadlines apply to different enforcement mechanisms under the Building Act 1984, and confusing them is a common and serious error
Practical application:
A frequent scenario: an owner disputes an enforcement notice, believing too much time has passed for the local authority to act. Assessors want you to explain the correct current time limits precisely — and to recognise that recent legislative change (the Building Safety Act 2022) significantly altered these limits, meaning outdated assumptions can lead to seriously wrong advice.

sections.h: 11B.9 Sustainability in Building Control Practice
sections.body:
Sustainability is directly relevant to Building Control, given the pathway's role in checking compliance with energy conservation and environmental standards at every stage of construction.

Key areas:
  • Energy conservation compliance — a core part of the Building Regulations that Building Control surveyors check and enforce
  • Sustainable material and construction method assessment — relevant when assessing alternative solutions for regulatory compliance
  • Life cycle cost considerations — relevant when advising on sustainability-related design or remedial options
  • Regulatory evolution — building regulations relating to energy performance and sustainability are updated periodically, requiring Building Control surveyors to stay current
Practical application:
Be ready to discuss how you would assess and advise on a sustainability-related compliance question — for example, an alternative construction method proposed to meet energy conservation requirements — explaining both the regulatory compliance angle and the broader sustainability implications.

sections.h: 11B.10 APC Scenarios and Michael AI Guided Practice
sections.body:
This section is your space to practise applying everything above to realistic APC-style scenarios, working through them with Michael, your AI tutor.

Michael can run you through scenario-based questions specific to Building Control — an enforcement notice time limit query, a dangerous structure assessment, a disputed compliance finding, a sustainability-related compliance question — and probe your answers the way an assessor would: asking you to justify your reasoning, challenging your position, and pushing you past description into advice.

How to use this section effectively:
  • Bring real examples from your own PDR wherever possible — Michael will help you structure and sharpen them, but the substance should be yours
  • Practise the "what would you advise" follow-up, not just "what happened" — assessors mark judgement, not narrative
  • Use Michael to stress-test weak points — if you're less confident on enforcement time limits or recent Building Safety Act changes, spend deliberate time there rather than defaulting to your strongest area
Open a session with Michael now and work through at least three Building Control-specific scenarios before moving to the module assessment.

sections.h: 11B.11 Module Assessment
sections.body:
Complete the following ten questions to check your readiness for Module 12. These mirror the style and difficulty of real APC interview questions on the Building Control pathway — read each one as if a panel member had just asked it, and answer as you would in the room.

  1. An owner believes it's too late for the local authority to serve an enforcement notice on unauthorised work completed 18 months ago. Is this correct, and why?
  2. Explain the health and safety considerations specific to inspecting a potentially dangerous structure.
  3. An owner disputes a compliance finding and is unhappy about the potential cost of remedial works. How would you handle this conversation?
  4. Describe how your organisation prices and resources building control instructions in a competitive market.
  5. Explain a sustainability-related compliance question you might be asked to assess, and how you would approach it.
  6. Outline the difference between the time limits for prosecuting a building regulations contravention and for serving an enforcement notice requiring its removal.
  7. Describe the process and criteria for assessing a proposed alternative construction solution against building regulations requirements.
  8. Explain the appeal process available to an owner who disputes an enforcement notice.
  9. How would you approach the inspection and assessment of a fire-damaged structure, balancing thoroughness with personal safety?
  10. Explain why all Building Control candidates receive the "Chartered Building Control Surveyor" designation automatically, unlike most other pathways.
Once you've worked through all ten and are satisfied with your answers — ideally after testing them against Michael's follow-up questions — you're ready for Module 12: Revision, Mock Tests and APC Simulation.

sections.h: 11B.12 If You've Been Referred: What This Module Means for You
sections.body:
If you're working through this module because you were referred at a previous assessment, a few things are worth saying directly.

First: a referral is not a verdict on your competence as a Building Control professional. It's specific, actionable feedback about what didn't land clearly enough in a particular interview, on a particular day, in front of a particular panel. Most successful resit candidates aren't relearning their pathway from scratch — they're closing specific gaps identified in their referral report.

How to use this module differently on a resit

  • Go back to your actual referral report before you start, and map its specific feedback points against the sections in this module — if your referral cited a gap in, for example, conflict avoidance or business planning, prioritise that section rather than working through everything in the original order
  • Pay particular attention to section 11B.2 (pathway structure and competency selection) if your referral raised any concern about your competency declaration itself — sometimes a referral reflects a mismatch between claimed level and demonstrated depth, not a knowledge gap
  • Use the Module 12 scenario at the end as a genuine mock question, and ask Michael to specifically challenge you the way an assessor would on the point that was flagged in your referral
  • If your referral touched on presentation or communication rather than technical content, that's a mandatory-competency issue (Communication and negotiation) as much as a pathway-specific one — it's worth revisiting the relevant mandatory competency module alongside this one, not just the Building Control-specific material here

Referral rates on Building Control and every RICS pathway are a normal, expected part of the process — not a signal you're not cut out for chartered status. Treat this module as a targeted second pass, not a full restart, and go into your resit with a clear sense of exactly what changed since last time.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 AHA Rent Review Notice Validity — Rural Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
You’ve been instructed to serve a rent review notice on behalf of a landlord under an Agricultural Holdings Act 1986 tenancy. The tenant’s agent disputes that the notice is valid. Talk me through it.

Tests: Valuation, Agriculture, Landlord and Tenant. Comes up in most Rural interviews.

The model answer starts by separating the legal question from the valuation question — a rent review that hasn’t been validly triggered never gets to the point of discussing figures, and assessors want to see you check the foundations before building on them.

Key elements:

1. Regime identification. The first check is always which Act governs the tenancy — Agricultural Holdings Act 1986 tenancies (pre-1995) and Agricultural Tenancies Act 1995 Farm Business Tenancies follow different rent review mechanisms entirely, and applying the wrong one invalidates everything that follows.

2. Notice period and form. AHA rent reviews require notice within a specific window before the review date, and must be in the prescribed form — a notice served outside that window, or in the wrong form, is defective regardless of intent.

3. Valid service. How the notice was served, and to whom, matters as much as its content. Service on the wrong party, or by a method not permitted, can invalidate an otherwise correct notice.

4. The rent review basis. Under AHA s.12, the review is to open market rent on specific statutory assumptions and disregards — you need to be able to explain what’s assumed and what’s disregarded, not just quote a figure.

5. Third party determination. If the parties can’t agree, AHA rent disputes go to arbitration or independent expert determination — knowing which route applies and when to invoke it is part of the competency, not an afterthought.

6. Negotiation first. Formal determination is a last resort. Assessors want to hear that you tried to negotiate on the evidence before escalating.

How to frame this:

“I first established which regime applied by checking the tenancy commencement date, before doing anything else.”

“I confirmed the notice met the prescribed form and minimum notice period before advising my client to serve it.”

“When the tenant’s agent challenged validity, I checked the service method against the Act before responding, rather than assuming it was fine.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) the correct regime identified before anything else, 2) notice validity checked rather than assumed, 3) third party determination only used once negotiation had genuinely failed.

Get the notice wrong and the rent review dies before it starts — assessors are listening for whether you checked validity before you did anything else.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 HMRC Capital Allowances Enquiry — Taxation Allowances Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
HMRC opens a formal enquiry into a capital allowances claim you’ve prepared for a client’s new industrial unit. Talk me through your response.

Tests: Accounting principles and procedures, Capital allowances, Quantification and costing. Comes up in most Taxation Allowances interviews.

The model answer treats an HMRC enquiry as a test of your original working papers, not a fresh argument to construct — if the evidence trail was solid at the point of claim, the response is straightforward.

Key elements:

1. Working papers review. The first step is going back to your original apportionment methodology and confirming what was classified as qualifying expenditure, and why.

2. Structural vs plant and machinery. This is the grey area HMRC challenges most often — you need the case law tests fresh in mind, not just the headline categories.

3. Contemporaneous evidence. Cost breakdowns, specification documents, and invoices contemporaneous with the works carry far more weight than a reconstruction after the fact.

4. Enquiry process and timeline. HMRC enquiries follow a formal process with statutory deadlines for response — missing these has consequences independent of the merits of the claim.

5. Concede vs defend. Not every item is worth defending. Part of the competency is judging which marginal items to concede and which core claims to hold, rather than fighting everything reflexively.

6. Client communication. Managing expectations on cost, time, and outcome uncertainty throughout — an enquiry can run for months, and clients need realistic guidance, not false reassurance.

How to frame this:

“I went back to my original apportionment working papers before responding to HMRC, rather than constructing a new justification.”

“Where an item sat in the grey area between structure and plant, I revisited the relevant case law tests before taking a position.”

“I kept my client informed of realistic timescales and the possibility of partial concession from the outset.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) evidence-based response rather than defensive assumption, 2) correct reasoning on the structural/plant distinction, 3) transparent client management throughout.

A capital allowances claim is only as strong as the working papers behind it — assessors want to hear that you can defend your numbers, not just produce them.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 Party Wall Act Notice Dispute — Building Surveying Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
Your client is planning works that fall under the Party Wall etc. Act 1996, and a neighbour disputes your Notice. Talk me through it.

Tests: Legal/regulatory compliance, Building pathology, Contract administration. One of the most frequently tested Building Surveying scenarios.

The model answer treats the Party Wall Act as a procedural discipline first and a technical building question second — most disputes come from getting the process wrong, not the construction detail.

Key elements:

1. Correct notice type. Section 1 (new wall on the line of junction), Section 2 (works to an existing party wall), or Section 6 (excavation near a neighbouring structure) each apply to different works — the wrong section invalidates the notice.

2. Notice periods and service. Each section carries its own minimum notice period, and the notice must be properly served on all relevant owners.

3. The neighbour’s options. On receipt, the adjoining owner can consent, dissent and appoint their own surveyor, or dissent and agree to a joint surveyor — all at the building owner’s cost. Candidates need to explain this accurately, not vaguely.

4. The Award. Where surveyors are appointed, they produce a Party Wall Award covering the works, access, and protective measures — understanding what an Award does and doesn’t cover is core to the competency.

5. Schedule of condition. A schedule of condition before works start protects both parties and is standard good practice, not an optional extra.

6. Escalation. If appointed surveyors can’t agree, the Act provides for a third surveyor to resolve the matter — knowing this mechanism exists, and when it’s invoked, matters.

How to frame this:

“I confirmed which section of the Act applied to the specific works before drafting the Notice.”

“When the neighbour dissented, I explained their right to appoint their own surveyor at the building owner’s cost.”

“I made sure a schedule of condition was agreed before works started, to protect both parties from later disputes.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) correct section identified for the works in question, 2) the neighbour’s statutory rights explained accurately, 3) schedule of condition treated as standard practice.

Get the wrong section or skip the schedule of condition, and you’ve created the dispute you were trying to avoid — assessors are listening for procedural precision here.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 Payment and Pay Less Notice Mechanics — Quantity Surveying Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
You’re administering interim payments on a JCT contract and the employer wants to pay less than the sum in the contractor’s application. Talk me through what needs to happen.

Tests: Contract practice, Quantification and costing, Procurement and tendering. Comes up in almost every QS interview.

The model answer separates the valuation question from the notice mechanics entirely — under the Construction Act, getting the process wrong can override the true value of the work.

Key elements:

1. The notified sum principle. Under the Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 (as amended), the sum stated in a valid Payment Notice becomes the notified sum due, regardless of the underlying valuation, unless properly challenged.

2. Payment Notice deadlines. Whoever is responsible for issuing the Payment Notice must do so within the contractual deadline — if none is issued, the application sum becomes the default notified sum.

3. Pay Less Notice. A separate notice, with its own deadline and required content, is needed to pay less than the notified sum — get the timing or content wrong and the employer must pay the notified sum in full.

4. Smash and grab risk. Defective or late notices expose the employer to a “smash and grab” adjudication, where the full notified sum is recovered irrespective of the true value of the work.

5. Valuing the work properly. The underlying valuation still matters — it just can’t substitute for correct notice procedure if a dispute arises.

6. Client communication. Making sure the employer understands these deadlines are contractual and absolute, well before they’re at risk of being missed.

How to frame this:

“I made sure the Payment Notice was issued within the contractual deadline, regardless of whether the valuation was fully finalised.”

“When the employer wanted to pay less, I explained the separate Pay Less Notice deadline and the smash and grab risk of missing it.”

“I kept the valuation and the notice mechanics separate in my own mind, so a payment dispute never became a notice dispute.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) correct statutory notice mechanics explained, 2) deadlines treated as absolute rather than negotiable, 3) awareness of adjudication risk from defective notices.

Miss a Pay Less Notice deadline and the employer pays the full notified sum regardless of the true value of the work — assessors want to know you understand this is a process test, not just a valuation one.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 Section 25 Notice Validity — Commercial Real Estate Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
You’re instructed to serve a Section 25 notice on a tenant ahead of lease expiry, and the tenant’s advisor disputes whether it was validly served. Talk me through it.

Tests: Landlord and tenant, Legal/regulatory compliance, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Commercial Real Estate scenarios.

The model answer treats notice validity as a legal precision exercise, not paperwork — a defective Section 25 notice can hand the tenant rights they shouldn’t have, regardless of the landlord’s underlying intentions.

Key elements:

1. Notice type and timing. A Section 25 notice (landlord-initiated) must be served not less than six and not more than twelve months before the termination date specified — outside that window, the notice is invalid.

2. Prescribed form and content. The notice must be in the correct prescribed form, stating whether the landlord opposes renewal and, if so, on what grounds.

3. Valid service. Service must comply with Section 23 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927 (which governs how notices under the 1954 Act are validly served) — the wrong method or the wrong recipient can invalidate an otherwise correctly timed and worded notice.

4. Grounds for opposition. Where a landlord opposes renewal, this must be based on one of the Act’s specific statutory grounds — client preference alone is not a valid ground.

5. The negotiation window. Before matters reach court, there is normally a window to negotiate new terms directly, which is usually the client’s preferred outcome over contested proceedings.

6. Client communication. Managing the landlord’s expectations on timeline, cost, and the real risk to their security of tenure position if procedure isn’t followed exactly.

How to frame this:

“I checked the notice fell within the six-to-twelve month window before advising my client to serve it.”

“When service was challenged, I confirmed the method used was permitted under the Act before responding to the tenant’s advisor.”

“I made sure my client understood which statutory grounds, if any, were realistically available before we opposed renewal.”

Three things assessors tick: 1) correct notice type and timing window identified, 2) service validity checked rather than assumed, 3) any grounds for opposition grounded in the statutory test, not client preference.

Get the timing or service wrong on a Section 25 notice and the tenant may gain rights they shouldn’t have — assessors are testing whether you treat this as a legal precision exercise, not paperwork.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 Secured Lending Valuation and Professional Negligence — Valuation Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
A lender challenges your secured lending valuation six months after a loan default, alleging professional negligence. Talk me through your defence.

Tests: Valuation, Inspection, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Valuation scenarios.

The model answer treats a negligence allegation as a test of your file, not a test of whether your figure was right — valuation is a matter of professional judgement within a defensible range, and your defence rests on demonstrating that range was reasonably arrived at, properly evidenced, and properly recorded at the time.

Key elements:

1. Standard of care, not perfect hindsight. The legal test is whether a reasonably competent valuer, exercising reasonable skill and care at the time, could have reached a similar figure on the evidence then available — not whether your figure matches what the market later showed the property was worth.

2. Red Book compliance at the time of valuation. Confirming the valuation met the mandatory minimum reporting requirements under VPS 3 — purpose, basis of value, extent of investigation, assumptions and special assumptions, valuation approach and reasoning, and date of valuation — is the first line of defence.

3. Inspection and investigation record. VPS 2 requires proper records of inspections and investigations to maintain a clear audit trail — file notes, photographs, and a record of what was and was not verified are what actually protect you months or years later, not memory.

4. Comparable evidence hierarchy. Being able to show the comparables relied on at the valuation date, and where they sat in the hierarchy of evidence, demonstrates the figure was reasoned rather than arbitrary.

5. Assumptions and special assumptions. Where any assumption was made — about tenure, condition, or planning status — showing it was reasonable to make at the time, and was clearly disclosed in the report, is central to a defence.

6. Early engagement with PII insurers. Notifying your professional indemnity insurers promptly on receiving a negligence allegation is standard professional discipline — delay can itself create problems independent of the merits of the claim.

How to frame this:

I went back to my valuation file first, to confirm what evidence and assumptions were recorded at the time, before responding to the allegation.

I checked the report against the VPS 3 minimum reporting requirements to confirm it was Red Book compliant at the point it was issued.

I notified my professional indemnity insurers as soon as the allegation was raised, rather than trying to resolve it informally first.

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding that the standard is reasonable care, not hindsight accuracy, 2) evidence of contemporaneous record-keeping and Red Book compliance, 3) recognising the professional discipline of prompt insurer notification.

A valuation is not negligent because the market later proved it wrong — it is negligent if a reasonably competent valuer could not have reached it on the evidence at the time. Assessors are testing whether you understand that distinction, not whether you can guarantee a figure will hold up forever.

m12PathwaySections.h: 12.16 NEC Compensation Event Time Bar — Infrastructure Pathway
m12PathwaySections.body:
Your contractor believes they have a valid compensation event under an NEC contract, but seven weeks have passed since they became aware of it and no notification has been submitted. Talk me through the situation and what you would advise.

Tests: Contract practice, Risk management, Client care. One of the most frequently tested Infrastructure scenarios.

The model answer treats the NEC compensation event notification period as an absolute contractual deadline, not a general guideline — under NEC3/NEC4 clause 61.3, missing it doesn't weaken the contractor's claim, it extinguishes it entirely, regardless of how genuine the underlying entitlement is.

Key elements:

1. The eight-week time bar is absolute. Under clause 61.3, if the contractor doesn't notify a compensation event within eight weeks of becoming aware of it, they lose all entitlement to a change in the prices, completion date, or key date for that event — there is no partial or proportionate outcome.

2. The exception that doesn't apply here. The time bar doesn't apply where the project manager should have notified the event under clause 61.1 (events arising from an instruction, certificate, or changed decision) but failed to — that's a narrow exception, not a general safety net, and doesn't rescue a contractor-side event the contractor was aware of.

3. "Becoming aware" is the trigger, not the event itself. The clock starts from when the contractor became aware the event happened, which can itself be a point of genuine dispute — but with one week left, this is not the moment to start litigating that question; it's the moment to notify immediately.

4. Urgent, unambiguous advice is needed now. With one week remaining, the professional priority is making sure the notification is submitted correctly and immediately — not debating the merits of the underlying claim, which can be assessed afterwards.

5. The employer-side incentive. It's worth understanding that the time bar operates in the employer's favour — some project managers may be inclined to let a deadline lapse rather than proactively remind the contractor, which is a live commercial dynamic on the other side of this scenario.

6. Document everything from this point. Whatever the outcome, the advice given and the timeline of events from this point forward should be clearly documented, given how commercially significant a missed deadline is.

How to frame this:

"I would advise the contractor to submit the notification immediately, regardless of any uncertainty about the exact date of awareness."

"I'd check whether this event falls under the project manager's own notification duty under clause 61.1, since that's the only exception to the time bar."

"I would not spend the remaining time debating the merits of the claim — that can be assessed after notification, but the deadline itself can't be recovered once missed."

Three things assessors tick: 1) understanding that the eight-week bar is binary, not proportionate, 2) correctly identifying the narrow clause 61.1 exception rather than treating it as a general safety net, 3) prioritising immediate action over debating the underlying merits with time running out.
